passages.title: On facing death without logical tricks
passages.text: Philosophy must be set around us, a wall that cannot be stormed, which Fortune, though she has assailed it with many siege engines, does not get past. The mind that has abandoned external things stands in a place that cannot be scaled, and claims its freedom in its own citadel; every missile falls below it. Fortune does not have the long hands we think she has: she seizes no one except the one who clings to her.

passages.title: On rejecting even moderate passions
passages.text: But what madness this is: to believe that where the beginnings of things are placed outside our control, their limits are within our control! How am I strong enough to set a limit to a thing that I was not strong enough to prevent, when it is easier to shut things out than to hold them down once they have been let in?

passages.title: On the divisions of philosophy
passages.text: Whichever of the three is missing throws the rest into disorder as well. For what use is it to have everything assessed, if you go too far in impulse? What use is it to have checked your impulses and to have your desires in your own power, if in the action itself you are ignorant of the timing and do not know when each thing should be done, and where, and how? For it is one thing to know the worth and the prices of things, another to know the critical moments, another to rein in impulses and to go to what has to be done, not rush at it. So a life is in harmony with itself when action does not desert impulse, and impulse takes its start from the worth of each thing, slack [or] keener in proportion as that thing is worth seeking.

passages.title: On whether the virtues are living beings
passages.text: No rational living being does anything unless it has first been stirred by the impression of some thing, then has formed an impulse, and then assent has confirmed this impulse. I will say what assent is. I ought to walk: only then do I walk, when I have said this to myself and approved this opinion of mine; I ought to sit: only then do I sit. This assent is not found in virtue.

passages.title: On the divisions of philosophy
passages.text: So, since philosophy has three parts, let us begin by setting out its moral part first. It has been held that this in turn is divided into three: the first is the examination that assigns to each thing its own and assesses how much each is worth, and it is useful in the highest degree (for what is so necessary as putting prices on things?); the second is about impulse, the third about actions. For the first thing is that you judge how much each thing is worth; the second, that you take up an ordered and moderated impulse towards those things; the third, that your impulse and your action fit together, so that in all of these you agree with yourself.

passages.title: On the oath to philosophy and reason
passages.text: You will not show me anyone who knows how he began to want what he wants: he was not led to it by deliberation but flung into it by impulse. Fortune collides with us no less often than we with it. It is shameful not to go but to be carried, and suddenly, in the middle of the whirlwind of things, to ask in a daze, “How did I get here?” Farewell.

passages.title: On philosophy as the guide of life
passages.text: But now is not the time to cross over into this discussion: what is ours to decide if providence is in command, or if the chain of the fates drags us along bound, or if the sudden and the unforeseen are the masters. I return now to this: to warn you and urge you not to let the impulse of your mind slip away and grow cold. Keep hold of it and set it firm, so that what is an impulse becomes a settled state of mind.

passages.title: On rejecting even moderate passions
passages.text: Next, if you grant any rights to sadness, to fear, to desire, to the other wrong movements, they will not be in our power. Why? Because the things that provoke them are outside us; and so they will grow according to whether the causes that stir them up are great or lesser. Fear will be greater if it has seen more to terrify it, or seen it nearer; desire will be keener to the degree that the hope of a larger thing has called it out.

passages.title: On removing the passions altogether
passages.text: It has often been asked whether it is better to have moderate passions or none. Our school drives them out; the Peripatetics temper them. For my part, I do not see how any moderate degree of a disease can be wholesome or useful. Do not be afraid: I am taking from you none of the things that you do not want denied to you. I will show myself easy and indulgent towards the things you are aiming at and that you think either necessary for life or useful or pleasant: I will take away the vice. For when I have forbidden you to crave, I will allow you to want, so that you may do those same things unafraid, so that you may do them with a surer purpose, so that you may feel the pleasures themselves more. Why should they not reach you more if you command them than if you are their slave?

claims.t: It is up to me what is in my soul: I keep my ruling part in my own power, and no one can rob me of the power to choose.
claims.shared: Two passages say that this is in my own hands: 8.27 that “it is up to me” that my soul be free of wickedness and craving, 9.6 that I am to keep the ruling part “in one’s own power”. In the Greek they use the same Stoic phrase for what is in a person’s own power. 11.31 adds that no one can rob me of the power to choose.
claims.changed: 9.6 is an instruction (“To keep the ruling part in one’s own power”); the claim says “I keep”. The translators allow “in its own power” as well. 11.31 is a saying of Epictetus that Marcus copied out; the claim makes it first person. 8.27 lists what is to be kept out of the soul (wickedness, craving, disturbance); the claim keeps only “what is in my soul”.

support.quote: Now it is up to me that in this soul there be no wickedness, no craving and no disturbance at all
support.follows: Keeping wickedness, craving and disturbance out of my soul is in my own power.
gives: It is up to me
what is in my soul

support.quote: To keep the ruling part in one’s own power.
support.follows: The ruling part can be kept in one’s own power, and one is to keep it there.
gives: It is up to me
I keep my ruling part in my own power

support.quote: There is no robber of the power to choose.
support.follows: No one can take a person’s power to choose away from them.
gives: no one can rob me of the power to choose

claims.t: Whatever others do, my mind cannot be harmed when it is gathered into itself and free of passions. It stays so while I take refuge in it and guard myself at every hour.
claims.shared: Both passages give the mind an image of something that cannot be harmed: in 8.46 a citadel that cannot be taken (“beyond capture”), in 8.50 a spring that washes out the mud thrown into it and “will in no way be stained”. Both also make it depend on me: in 8.46 I must flee to it, in 8.50 I must guard myself at every hour.
claims.changed: Each passage has its own image, a fortress and a spring; the claim keeps neither and says what they share. “Whatever others do” rests on 8.50 alone, which says “they kill, they cut up like meat, they hound with curses” without saying who; the claim says “others”.

support.quote: Remember that the ruling part becomes unconquerable when, gathered into itself, it is content with itself
support.follows: The ruling part cannot be conquered when it is gathered into itself and content with itself.
gives: my mind cannot be harmed
when it is gathered into itself

support.quote: This is why the mind free of passions is a citadel, for a human being has nothing better fortified to flee to, where they would from then on be beyond capture.
support.follows: A mind free of passions is a fortress: whoever flees to it cannot be captured.
gives: my mind cannot be harmed
free of passions
while I take refuge in it

support.quote: They kill, they cut up like meat, they hound with curses. What, then, is that to the mind staying clean, sane, self-controlled, just?
support.follows: Killing, butchering and cursing have no bearing on whether the mind stays clean, sane, self-controlled and just.
gives: Whatever others do
my mind cannot be harmed

support.quote: even if they throw in mud, even if dung, it will very quickly scatter these and wash them out, and will in no way be stained
support.follows: A clear spring quickly washes away mud or dung thrown into it and is not stained by them.
gives: my mind cannot be harmed

support.quote: If you guard yourself at every hour so as to be free
support.follows: The mind stays an ever-flowing spring if I guard myself at every hour so as to be free.
gives: guard myself at every hour

claims.t: I keep wiping out impressions, and any turn my mind takes that I should guard against. As I wipe each one away, I say a sentence to myself over it.
claims.shared: Three passages give the same command in the same words: “Wipe out the impression” (7.21), “Keep wiping out impressions” (8.27), “To wipe out an impression” (9.6). 8.27 and 11.17 both add that something is to be said while wiping: “saying to yourself continually” and “saying over each one”.
claims.changed: 11.17 wipes away four “turns” of the ruling part, not impressions; the first of them is an imagining, the others are a thought that dissolves community, words not my own, and giving way to the body. The claim names both impressions and turns, and does not say that every turn is an impression.

support.quote: Wipe out the impression.
support.follows: An impression can be wiped out, and Marcus tells himself to do it.
gives: I keep wiping out impressions

support.quote: Keep wiping out impressions, saying to yourself continually
support.follows: Wiping out impressions is to be done again and again, while saying something to oneself.
gives: I keep wiping out impressions
As I wipe each one away, I say a sentence to myself over it

support.quote: To wipe out an impression.
support.follows: Wiping out an impression is one of the things a person can do.
gives: I keep wiping out impressions

support.quote: Four turns that the ruling part takes must above all be guarded against without a break and, whenever you catch them, wiped away, saying over each one as follows:
support.follows: Four turns of the ruling part are to be watched for and wiped away when caught, with a sentence said over each.
gives: any turn my mind takes that I should guard against
As I wipe each one away, I say a sentence to myself over it

claims.t: I can stop an impulse, and each impulse I form is for the common good and has a reservation: if nothing prevents it. I go by the worth of each thing; with each impulse I give what is just, and I keep desire out altogether.
claims.shared: 11.31 asks that impulses be “according to worth”, and 8.27 that I use each thing “according to its worth”: both go by the worth of each thing. 9.6 and 11.31 both keep desire out: “To quench desire” and “keep away from desire altogether”.
claims.changed: “If nothing prevents it” is the editor’s gloss on “with a reservation”, the Stoic sense the translators give for the word; no passage spells it out. 6.45 shows it in use (claim 6): when I am blocked, I was not desiring what is impossible. 11.31 speaks of the worth of what an impulse aims at, 8.27 of the worth of the things I use; the claim says “each thing” to cover both. 11.31 gives Epictetus’s rule; the claim makes it mine. 6.45 speaks of “desiring” an impulse, which sits uneasily with keeping away from desire altogether; the claim follows 9.6 and 11.31 on desire.

support.quote: To stop an impulse.
support.follows: An impulse can be stopped, and one is to stop it.
gives: I can stop an impulse

support.quote: in the field of the impulses keep up attention, so that they are with a reservation, so that they are social, so that they are according to worth
support.follows: Impulses must be watched so that each carries a reservation, serves the community and matches the worth of its object.
gives: each impulse I form is for the common good and has a reservation
I go by the worth of each thing

support.quote: seeing what kind of thing everything is, I use each according to its worth
support.follows: Once I see what kind of thing each thing is, I deal with each according to its worth.
gives: I go by the worth of each thing

support.quote: at every impulse to give what is just
support.follows: With every impulse I should give what is just.
gives: with each impulse I give what is just

support.quote: To quench desire.
support.follows: Desire can be put out, as a fire is put out.
gives: I keep desire out

support.quote: keep away from desire altogether
support.follows: One is to keep away from desire entirely.
gives: I keep desire out

claims.t: Nothing I do is careless: I do no act at random, but by a rule of the art of living. I do not wander among my impressions, and with each one I keep the sure grasp: I hold to what is so clear that it cannot be false.
claims.shared: 4.2 and 8.49 both forbid carelessness in acts: “no act be done at random” and “Not to be slovenly in actions”. 4.18 and 8.49 both forbid wandering: “Not to roam away” and “not to wander in impressions”.
claims.changed: 4.2 says “the art” and does not name it; “of living” is the editor’s. 4.18 does not say where one roams; “among my impressions” is 8.49’s. 4.18’s “sure grasp” is a Stoic term: an impression that grasps its object so clearly that it cannot be false. The words after “the sure grasp” are the editor’s explanation of it, from the translators’ note.

support.quote: Let no act be done at random, or otherwise than according to a rule that goes to make up the art.
support.follows: Every act should follow a rule that belongs to the art, and none should be done at random.
gives: Nothing I do is careless
I do no act at random, but by a rule

support.quote: Not to be slovenly in actions
support.follows: My actions should not be slovenly.
gives: Nothing I do is careless

support.quote: not to wander in impressions
support.follows: I should not let myself wander from one impression to another.
gives: I do not wander
among my impressions

support.quote: Not to roam away
support.follows: I should not roam off course.
gives: I do not wander

support.quote: at every impression to keep the sure grasp
support.follows: With every impression I should keep the sure grasp.
gives: with each one I keep the sure grasp

claims.role: When I am kept from something
claims.t: When I am kept from something, I am content and free of distress, and I turn the hindrance to another virtue: one that is still possible. I remember that my impulse had its reservation, and that I was not desiring what is impossible.
claims.shared: Both passages begin from something that cannot be done: in 6.45 someone “stands in the way”, in 8.7 “It is not possible to read”. Both turn from it to a virtue that remains: 6.45 to “another virtue”, 8.7 to holding back insolence and mastering pleasures and pains.
claims.changed: 6.45 is about a just act blocked by force; 8.7 does not say what keeps Marcus from reading. The claim says only “kept from something”. Only 6.45 ties the block to the reservation of claim 4.

support.quote: If, however, someone uses force and stands in the way, change over to being content and free of distress, and use the hindrance for another virtue
support.follows: When someone forcibly blocks what I set out to do, I should be content and use the hindrance to practise another virtue.
gives: When I am kept from something
I am content and free of distress, and I turn the hindrance to another virtue

support.quote: remember that your impulse was with a reservation, and that you were not desiring what is impossible
support.follows: When blocked, I am to remember that my impulse had a reservation and that I was not desiring the impossible.
gives: I remember that my impulse had its reservation, and that I was not desiring what is impossible

support.quote: It is not possible to read. But it is possible to hold back insolence. But it is possible to get the better of pleasures and pains.
support.follows: Reading may not be possible, but holding back insolence and getting the better of pleasures and pains still are.
gives: When I am kept from something
one that is still possible

single.quote: is not about just anything, but about being mad or not
single.label: What is at stake
single.t: In governing my impressions, impulses and desires, I am contending for no small matter: it is whether I am sane or mad.
single.why: Only this passage names what the struggle is about. 8.50 calls the mind “sane”, but it does not speak of a contest.
single.follows: Epictetus says the contest is about being mad or not, not about some ordinary matter.

single.quote: The wrong that person did, leave it there, where the wrong came to be.
single.label: Another’s wrong
single.t: When someone does wrong, I leave the wrong with them, where it came to be.
single.why: Only this passage says where another person’s wrong belongs. 8.7 speaks of not being angry with the ungrateful, which is a different point.
single.follows: A wrong stays with the one who did it, and I should leave it there.

single.quote: But it is possible not to be angry with the insensitive and the ungrateful, and more than that, to care for them.
single.label: The ungrateful
single.t: I can keep from being angry with people who are insensitive or ungrateful, and more than that, I can care for them.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of anger at other people and of caring for them instead.
single.follows: It is possible not to be angry with the insensitive and ungrateful, and even to care for them.

single.quote: “This imagining is not necessary.” “This one dissolves community.” “This thing you are about to say is not from yourself.”
single.label: Three sentences
single.t: When I catch my mind taking a turn I should guard against, I say one of three sentences over it: that this imagining is not necessary, that this thought dissolves community, or that what I am about to say is not from myself.
single.why: Only this passage gives these three sentences. 8.27 gives a different sentence, which this article quotes in claim 1.
single.follows: Each of three turns has its sentence: this imagining is not needed, this breaks community, these words are not my own.

single.quote: The fourth is the one for which you will reproach yourself: that this is the mark of the more divine part in you being beaten and lying down under the less worthy and mortal portion, that of the body, and under its rough or smooth movements.
single.label: Beaten by the body
single.t: When the body and its pains or pleasures get the better of me, the more divine part of me is beaten and lies down under the lesser, mortal part, and I reproach myself for it.
single.why: Only this passage says what it looks like when the ruling part loses. 8.7 says it is possible to get the better of pleasures and pains, but not what losing is.
single.follows: When the more divine part gives way to the body and its movements, it has been beaten, and that is a cause for self-reproach.

members.text:
Wipe off all opinion stay the force and violence of unreasonable
lusts and affections: circumscribe the present time examine whatsoever
it be that is happened, either to thyself or to another: divide all
present objects, either in that which is formal or material think of the
last hour. That which thy neighbour hath committed, where the guilt of
it lieth, there let it rest. Examine in order whatsoever is spoken. Let
thy mind penetrate both into the effects, and into the causes. Rejoice
thyself with true simplicity, and modesty; and that all middle things
between virtue and vice are indifferent unto thee. Finally, love
mankind; obey God.
members.english:
Wipe out the impression. Stop the pulling of the puppet strings. Draw a line around the present time. Recognise what is happening, whether to you or to another. Take the thing before you apart and divide it into what is cause and what is material. Think of the last hour. The wrong that person did, leave it there, where the wrong came to be.

To stretch thinking out alongside what is being said. To have the mind get inside the things that come about and the things that act.

Brighten yourself with simplicity and modesty and with indifference towards what lies between virtue and vice. Love the human race. Follow god.
members.greek:
Ἐξάλειψον τὴν φαντασίαν. στῆσον τὴν νευροσπαστίαν. περίγραψον τὸ ἐνεστὼς τοῦ χρόνου. γνώρισον τὸ συμβαῖνον ἢ σοὶ ἢ ἄλλῳ. δίελε καὶ μέρισον τὸ ὑποκείμενον εἰς τὸ αἰτιῶδες καὶ ὑλικόν. ἐννόησον τὴν ἐσχάτην ὥραν. τὸ ἐκείνῳ ἁμαρτηθὲν ἐκεῖ κατάλιπε ὅπου ἡ ἁμαρτία ὑπέστη.

Συμπαρεκτείνειν τὴν νόησιν τοῖς λεγομένοις. εἰσδύεσθαι τὸν νοῦν εἰς τὰ γινόμενα καὶ ποιοῦντα.

Φαίδρυνον σεαυτὸν ἁπλότητι καὶ αἰδοῖ καὶ τῇ πρὸς τὸ ἀνὰ μέσον ἀρετῆς καὶ κακίας ἀδιαφορίᾳ. φίλησον τὸ ἀνθρώπινον γένος. ἀκολούθησον θεῷ.

members.text:
Four several dispositions or inclinations there be of the mind and
understanding, which to be aware of, thou must carefully observe: and
whensoever thou doest discover them, thou must rectify them, saying to
thyself concerning every one of them, This imagination is not necessary;
this is uncharitable: this thou shalt speak as another man's slave, or
instrument; than which nothing can be more senseless and absurd: for
the fourth, thou shalt sharply check and upbraid thyself; for that
thou doest suffer that more divine part in thee, to become subject and
obnoxious to that more ignoble part of thy body, and the gross lusts
and concupiscences thereof.
members.english: Four turns that the ruling part takes must above all be guarded against without a break and, whenever you catch them, wiped away, saying over each one as follows: “This imagining is not necessary.” “This one dissolves community.” “This thing you are about to say is not from yourself.” For count it among the most absurd things not to speak from yourself. The fourth is the one for which you will reproach yourself: that this is the mark of the more divine part in you being beaten and lying down under the less worthy and mortal portion, that of the body, and under its rough or smooth movements.
members.greek: Τέσσαρας μάλιστα τροπὰς τοῦ ἡγεμονικοῦ παραφυλακτέον διηνεκῶς καὶ ἐπειδὰν φωράσῃς ἀπαλειπτέον, ἐπιλέγοντα ἐφ’ ἑκάστου οὕτως· τοῦτο τὸ φάντασμα οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον· τοῦτο λυτικὸν κοινωνίας· τοῦτο οὐκ ἀπὸ σαυτοῦ μέλλεις λέγειν· τὸ γὰρ μὴ ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ λέγειν ἐν τοῖς ἀτοπωτάτοις νόμιζε. τέταρτον δέ ἐστι, καθὸ σεαυτῷ ὀνειδιεῖς, ὅτι τοῦτο ἡττωμένου ἐστὶ καὶ ὑποκατακλινομένου τοῦ ἐν σοὶ θειοτέρου μέρους τῇ ἀτιμοτέρᾳ καὶ θνητῇ μοίρᾳ, τῇ τοῦ σώματος καὶ ταῖς τούτου τραχείαις ἢ λείαις κινήσεσιν.

members.text:
Wipe off all idle fancies, and say unto thyself incessantly; Now
if I will, it is in my power to keep out of this my soul all wickedness,
all lust, and concupiscences, all trouble and confusion. But on the
contrary to behold and consider all things according to their true
nature, and to carry myself towards everything according to its true
worth. Remember then this thy power that nature hath given thee.
members.english: Keep wiping out impressions, saying to yourself continually: “Now it is up to me that in this soul there be no wickedness, no craving and no disturbance at all, but that, seeing what kind of thing everything is, I use each according to its worth.” Remember this power in accordance with nature.
members.greek: Ἐξάλειφε τὰς φαντασίας συνεχῶς σεαυτῷ λέγων· νῦν ἐπ’ ἐμοί ἐστιν ἵνα ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ψυχῇ μηδεμία πονηρία ᾖ μηδὲ ἐπιθυμία μηδὲ ὅλως ταραχή τις, ἀλλὰ βλέπων πάντα ὁποῖά ἐστι χρῶμαι ἑκάστῳ κατ’ ἀξίαν. μέμνησο ταύτης τῆς ἐξουσίας κατὰ φύσιν.

members.text:
Let us do our best endeavours to persuade them; but however, if
reason and justice lead thee to it, do it, though they be never so much
against it. But if any shall by force withstand thee, and hinder thee in
it, convert thy virtuous inclination from one object unto another, from
justice to contented equanimity, and cheerful patience: so that what in
the one is thy hindrance, thou mayst make use of it for the exercise of
another virtue: and remember that it was with due exception, and
reservation, that thou didst at first incline and desire. For thou didst
not set thy mind upon things impossible. Upon what then? that all thy
desires might ever be moderated with this due kind of reservation. And
this thou hast, and mayst always obtain, whether the thing desired be in
thy power or no. And what do I care for more, if that for which I was
born and brought forth into the world (to rule all my desires with
reason and discretion) may be?
members.english: Try to persuade them, but act even against their will whenever the reasoning of justice leads that way. If, however, someone uses force and stands in the way, change over to being content and free of distress, and use the hindrance for another virtue; and remember that your impulse was with a reservation, and that you were not desiring what is impossible. What were you desiring, then? An impulse of some such kind. And this you attain: the things we were led forward for, these come about.
members.greek: Πειρῶ μὲν πείθειν αὐτούς, πρᾶττε δὲ καὶ ἀκόντων, ὅταν τῆς δικαιοσύνης ὁ λόγος οὕτως ἄγῃ. ἐὰν μέντοι βίᾳ τις προσχρώμενος ἐνίστηται, μετάβαινε ἐπὶ τὸ εὐάρεστον καὶ ἄλυπον καὶ συγχρῶ εἰς ἄλλην ἀρετὴν τῇ κωλύσει, καὶ μέμνησο ὅτι μεθ’ ὑπεξαιρέσεως ὥρμας καὶ ὅτι τῶν ἀδυνάτων οὐκ ὠρέγου. τίνος οὖν; τῆς τοιᾶσδέ τινος ὁρμῆς. τούτου δὲ τυγχάνεις· ἐφ’ οἷς προήχθημεν, ταῦτα γίνεται.

members.text:
Remember that thy mind is of that nature as that it becometh
altogether unconquerable, when once recollected in herself, she seeks no
other content than this, that she cannot be forced: yea though it so
fall out, that it be even against reason itself, that it cloth bandy.
How much less when by the help of reason she is able to judge of things
with discretion? And therefore let thy chief fort and place of defence
be, a mind free from passions. A stronger place, (whereunto to make his
refuge, and so to become impregnable) and better fortified than this,
hath no man. He that seeth not this is unlearned. He that seeth it, and
betaketh not himself to this place of refuge, is unhappy.
members.english: Remember that the ruling part becomes unconquerable when, gathered into itself, it is content with itself, not doing anything it does not want to do, even if it takes its stand without reason. What, then, when it judges about something with reason as well, and after looking all round it? This is why the mind free of passions is a citadel, for a human being has nothing better fortified to flee to, where they would from then on be beyond capture. So whoever has not seen this is ignorant, and whoever has seen it and does not flee to it is unfortunate.
members.greek: Μέμνησο ὅτι ἀκαταμάχητον γίνεται τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, ὅταν εἰς ἑαυτὸ συστραφὲν ἀρκεσθῇ ἑαυτῷ, μὴ ποιοῦν τι ὃ μὴ θέλει, κἂν ἀλόγως παρατάξηται. τί οὖν, ὅταν καὶ μετὰ λόγου καὶ περιεσκεμμένως κρίνῃ περί τινος; διὰ τοῦτο ἀκρόπολίς ἐστιν ἡ ἐλευθέρα παθῶν διάνοια· οὐδὲν γὰρ ὀχυρώτερον ἔχει ἄνθρωπος, ἐφ’ ὃ καταφυγὼν ἀνάλωτος λοιπὸν ἂν εἴη. ὁ μὲν οὖν μὴ ἑωρακὼς τοῦτο ἀμαθής, ὁ δὲ ἑωρακὼς καὶ μὴ καταφεύγων ἀτυχής.

members.text:
Not to be slack and negligent; or loose, and wanton in thy
actions; nor contentious, and troublesome in thy conversation; nor to
rove and wander in thy fancies and imaginations. Not basely to contract
thy soul; nor boisterously to sally out with it, or furiously to launch
out as it were, nor ever to want employment.
members.english: Not to be slovenly in actions, not to make a muddle in dealings with people, not to wander in impressions, not to shrink together or leap out in the soul at all, not to be without leisure in life.
members.greek: Μήτε ἐν ταῖς πράξεσιν ἐπισύρειν μήτε ἐν ταῖς ὁμιλίαις φύρειν μήτε ἐν ταῖς φαντασίαις ἀλᾶσθαι μήτε τῇ ψυχῇ καθάπαξ συνέλκεσθαι ἢ ἐκθόρνυσθαι μήτε ἐν τῷ βίῳ ἀσχολεῖσθαι.

members.text:
'Of the free will there is no thief or robber:' out of Epictetus;
Whose is this also: that we should find a certain art and method of
assenting; and that we should always observe with great care and heed
the inclinations of our minds, that they may always be with their due
restraint and reservation, always charitable, and according to the
true worth of every present object. And as for earnest longing, that we
should altogether avoid it: and to use averseness in those things only,
that wholly depend of our own wills. It is not about ordinary petty
matters, believe it, that all our strife and contention is, but whether,
with the vulgar, we should be mad, or by the help of philosophy wise and
sober, said he.
members.english:
“There is no robber of the power to choose.” That is the saying of Epictetus.

“One must find an art,” he said, “for giving assent, and in the field of the impulses keep up attention, so that they are with a reservation, so that they are social, so that they are according to worth; and keep away from desire altogether, and use aversion towards none of the things that are not up to us.”

“So the contest,” he said, “is not about just anything, but about being mad or not.”
members.greek:
Λῃστὴς προαιρέσεως οὐ γίνεται· τὸ τοῦ Ἐπικτήτου.

Τέχνην, ἔφη, δεῖ περὶ τὸ συγκατατίθεσθαι εὑρεῖν καὶ ἐν τῷ περὶ τὰς ὁρμὰς τόπῳ τὸ προσεκτικὸν φυλάσσειν, ἵνα μεθ’ ὑπεξαιρέσεως, ἵνα κοινωνικαί, ἵνα κατ’ ἀξίαν, καὶ ὀρέξεως μὲν παντάπασιν ἀπέχεσθαι, ἐκκλίσει δὲ πρὸς μηδὲν τῶν οὐκ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν χρῆσθαι.

Οὐ περὶ τοῦ τυχόντος οὖν, ἔφη, ἐστὶν ὁ ἀγών, ἀλλὰ περὶ τοῦ μαίνεσθαι ἢ μή.

members.text:
Not to wander out of the way, but upon every motion and desire,
to perform that which is just: and ever to be careful to attain to the
true natural apprehension of every fancy, that presents itself.
members.english: Not to roam away, but at every impulse to give what is just, and at every impression to keep the sure grasp.
members.greek: Μὴ ἀπορρέμβεσθαι, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ πάσης ὁρμῆς τὸ δίκαιον ἀποδιδόναι καὶ ἐπὶ πάσης φαντασίας σῴζειν τὸ καταληπτικόν.

members.text:
'They kill me, they cut my flesh; they persecute my person with
curses.' What then? May not thy mind for all this continue pure,
prudent, temperate, just? As a fountain of sweet and clear water, though
she be cursed by some stander by, yet do her springs nevertheless still
run as sweet and clear as before; yea though either dirt or dung be
thrown in, yet is it no sooner thrown, than dispersed, and she cleared.
She cannot be dyed or infected by it. What then must I do, that I
may have within myself an overflowing fountain, and not a well? Beget
thyself by continual pains and endeavours to true liberty with charity,
and true simplicity and modesty.
members.english: They kill, they cut up like meat, they hound with curses. What, then, is that to the mind staying clean, sane, self-controlled, just? It is as if someone stood beside a clear, sweet spring and insulted it, yet it does not stop welling up with water fit to drink; even if they throw in mud, even if dung, it will very quickly scatter these and wash them out, and will in no way be stained. How, then, will you have an ever-flowing spring and not a well? If you guard yourself at every hour so as to be free, and with that to act kindly, simply and modestly.
members.greek: Κτείνουσι, κρεανομοῦσι, κατάραις ἐλαύνουσι. τί οὖν ταῦτα πρὸς τὸ τὴν διάνοιαν μένειν καθαράν, φρενήρη, σώφρονα, δικαίαν; οἷον εἴ τις παραστὰς πηγῇ διαυγεῖ καὶ γλυκείᾳ βλασφημοίη αὐτήν, ἡ δὲ οὐ παύεται πότιμον ἀναβλύζουσα· κἂν πηλὸν ἐμβάλῃ, κἂν κοπρίαν, τάχιστα διασκεδάσει αὐτὰ καὶ ἐκκλύσει καὶ οὐδαμῶς βαφήσεται. πῶς οὖν πηγὴν ἀέναον ἕξεις καὶ μὴ φρέαρ; ἂν φυλάσσῃς σεαυτὸν πάσης ὥρας εἰς ἐλευθερίαν μετὰ τοῦ εὐμενῶς καὶ ἁπλῶς καὶ αἰδημόνως.

members.text:
Thou hast no time nor opportunity to read. What then? Hast thou
not time and opportunity to exercise thyself, not to wrong thyself; to
strive against all carnal pleasures and pains, and to get the upper hand
of them; to contemn honour and vainglory; and not only, not to be angry
with them, whom towards thee thou doest find unsensible and unthankful;
but also to have a care of them still, and of their welfare?
members.english: It is not possible to read. But it is possible to hold back insolence. But it is possible to get the better of pleasures and pains. But it is possible to be above petty reputation. But it is possible not to be angry with the insensitive and the ungrateful, and more than that, to care for them.
members.greek: Ἀναγινώσκειν οὐκ ἔξεστιν. ἀλλὰ ὕβριν ἀνείργειν ἔξεστιν· ἀλλὰ ἡδονῶν καὶ πόνων καθυπερτερεῖν ἔξεστιν· ἀλλὰ τοῦ δοξαρίου ὑπεράνω εἶναι ἔξεστιν· ἀλλὰ ἀναισθήτοις καὶ ἀχαρίστοις μὴ θυμοῦσθαι, προσέτι κήδεσθαι αὐτῶν ἔξεστιν.

members.text:
To wipe away fancy, to use deliberation, to quench concupiscence, to
keep the mind free to herself.
members.english: To wipe out an impression. To stop an impulse. To quench desire. To keep the ruling part in one’s own power.
members.greek: Ἐξαλεῖψαι φαντασίαν· στῆσαι ὁρμήν· σβέσαι ὄρεξιν· ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ ἔχειν τὸ ἡγεμονικόν.

members.text:
Let nothing be done rashly, and at random, but all things according
to the most exact and perfect rules of art.
members.english: Let no act be done at random, or otherwise than according to a rule that goes to make up the art.
members.greek: Μηδὲν ἐνέργημα εἰκῇ μηδὲ ἄλλως ἢ κατὰ θεώρημα συμπληρωτικὸν τῆς τέχνης ἐνεργείσθω.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 7.21 is 7.29–31a, 11.17 is 11.19, 8.27 is 8.29, 6.45 is 6.50, 8.46 is 8.48, 8.49 is 8.51a, 11.31 is 11.36–38, 4.18 is 4.22, 8.50 is 8.51b, 8.7 is 8.8 and 9.6 is 9.7; 4.2 is the same.
Calls the section “Wiping out impressions, checking impulses” instead of “Clearing away opinion and impulse”. No passage speaks of opinion; seven speak of impressions or impulses.
Puts 11.17’s four “turns” of the ruling part beside impressions in claim 3. Only the first turn, an imagining, is a kind of impression; the claim names both.

Explains “with a reservation” as “on condition that nothing prevents it” in the statement and as “if nothing prevents it” in claim 4. That is the Stoic sense the translators give for the word; no passage says it in these words. 6.45 shows it in use: when blocked, I was not desiring what is impossible (claim 6).
Reads 11.31 as Marcus’s own rule, though he gives it as the words of Epictetus.

Takes 11.17’s “rough or smooth movements” as the body’s pains and pleasures, as the translators do, and says “pains or pleasures” in the article; the quote keeps Marcus’s words. The wording of the Greek there has been doubted.

Keeps “If you guard yourself at every hour so as to be free” in 8.50 as the translators give it. They note, from memory and unchecked, that the verb has been doubted and “grow” proposed; with that reading, “guard myself at every hour” in claim 2 would lose its backing.

Leaves out, as repeats or as off this section’s topic: most of 7.21’s other commands (the puppet strings, drawing a line around the present time, the last hour, taking a thing apart into cause and matter, which is Article 4’s, and the closing words on simplicity and following god); 11.31’s “art for giving assent” and its rule on aversion; 8.27’s “Remember this power in accordance with nature”; and 8.7’s being above petty reputation.
articles.limit: Other articles say parts of this one. Wiping out a judgment once it is made is Article 7’s claim 3 and Article 8’s claim 2, and 5.2 in Article 18 says the same of impressions; this article adds the daily habit and the sentence said over each one. Article 8 says that setting out without “if nothing prevents it” is already bad, and that nothing from outside touches my mind (8.39 and claim 3); here the reservation becomes a rule for every impulse, and the mind’s safety depends on my guarding it. Article 12 says I can retreat into myself at any hour, and Article 13 that no one can prevent me from living well, both near claims 1 and 2. Leaving another’s wrong with them (7.21) is Article 28’s statement. Article 2 already says that dealing with an obstacle becomes my next action (claim 6), that I do not accept what is uncertain (near claim 5), and that reason should not be overpowered by the body; 11.17 here shows what it looks like when it is. Claim 4’s “for the common good” is close to Article 1’s claim 3. What this article adds is the exercise itself: wiping out impressions, forming impulses with a reservation, keeping desire out. Many of its passages are bare commands with no reason given, and the six claims read more as a list of exercises than as one thought.

articles.title: Good whatever others say, and open to being set right

statement.t: Whatever others say of me, I act well, and I change my mind only when I am shown what is true, just or of common benefit.

parts.words: Whatever others say of me, I act well
I change my mind
only when I am shown what is true, just or of common benefit

statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 hold the first half: talk does not move me, and my mind stands by itself. Claim 3 is the other half: a reason given by someone else does move me, and that too is my own act. Claim 4 shows the failure, wanting approval; claim 5 is a practice of openness to other minds.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the claims on being spoken ill of and on wanting approval gain a second author; the article gains, under “Why”, a reward that lies in the deed itself and, under “When it breaks”, an answer for one who cannot stand alone; and the claim that my mind stands upright by itself is limited, since he holds that no one comes up out of his folly unaided.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a motive: I act well whatever others say, change my mind only for what is true, just or of common benefit, and look for no reward, since the pay for a right deed is to have done it.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: But, by Hercules, you will often have to be just with a bad name
piece.follows: Acting justly will often go together with having a bad name, and a just person must accept that.
piece.context: Letter 113 ends on justice that wants no reward and no glory. Having “a bad name” is being spoken ill of while one is acting justly.

am spoken ill of

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Anyone who wants his virtue made public is working not for virtue but for glory.
piece.follows: Whoever wants his good conduct made known is working for glory, not for goodness.
piece.context: Letter 113, on justice: it is nothing to the point how many people know of one’s fairness. Here “his virtue” is the good conduct a person wants others to know of.
gives: I fail when I want to be approved of

items.label: why
items.t: I am good without looking for a reward. The reward of every virtue is in the virtue itself: the pay for a right deed is to have done it.
items.why: In this section Marcus says I must be good whatever others say; he does not say what I gain by it. Seneca says: nothing outside the right deed itself. 113.31 speaks of justice, 81.19 of all the virtues; the word “good” here rests on the second.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I ought to be just without payment.
support.follows: I ought to act justly without expecting anything in return.
support.context: Letter 113 ends on justice, which asks nothing from itself except to be put to use. Seneca says each person should first convince himself of this sentence.
gives: I am good without looking for a reward

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the reward of all the virtues is in the virtues themselves. For they are not practised for a prize: the pay for a right deed is to have done it.
support.follows: Virtues are not practised for payment; doing a right deed is its own payment.
support.context: Letter 81, on benefits: gratitude helps the grateful person, not because the favour comes back, but because a virtue is its own reward.
gives: The reward of every virtue is in the virtue itself
the pay for a right deed is to have done it

items.label: breaks
items.t: If I cannot find the way by myself, I can follow well where someone else has gone ahead; that is the second rank, and it is still outstanding. I need not look down on myself for needing help: wanting to be saved is a great deal.
items.why: Marcus already allows that I follow the one who sets me right (claim 3). Seneca adds that needing a guide is a lower rank but still outstanding, and nothing to look down on. He speaks of “the man”; here it becomes “I”.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Others, he says, need another’s aid: they will not go if no one has gone ahead, but they will follow well. Metrodorus, he says, is one of these; this too is an outstanding talent, but of the second rank.
support.follows: Some people go only when someone has gone ahead, and follow well; such a talent is outstanding too, though of the second rank.
support.context: Letter 52, on choosing teachers: Epicurus ranks those who reach the truth alone above those who need a guide. Seneca says he would be glad to be admitted to the second.
gives: I can follow well where someone else has gone ahead
that is the second rank, and it is still outstanding

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Do not look down even on the man who can be safe through another’s good offices; this too is a great deal, to want to be saved.
support.follows: Someone who can be safe through another’s help is not to be looked down on; wanting to be saved counts for much.
support.context: Letter 52, on choosing teachers. Being “safe” is being freed from folly, which Seneca has just said no one escapes unaided.
gives: I need not look down on myself for needing help
wanting to be saved is a great deal

items.t: Seneca says that no one is strong enough by himself to come up out of his folly: someone must stretch out a hand and draw him out. Marcus asks that my mind be upright by itself, not set upright. The editor reads the two as goal and route, so that Seneca limits Marcus and does not contradict him; Marcus too follows the one who sets him right (claim 3). Seneca is not consistent here: in the next section (Ep. 52.3) he reports Epicurus’s first grade, people who came out to the truth without anyone’s help.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: No one is strong enough by himself to come up to the surface; someone must stretch out a hand, someone must draw him out.
support.follows: No one is strong enough to come up out of his folly alone; he needs someone to stretch out a hand and draw him out.
support.context: Letter 52, on choosing teachers, opens on how we veer from plan to plan. Coming up “to the surface” is getting free of that folly, as Lucilius calls it.

amend.t: ; and I look for no reward, since the pay for a right deed is to have done it
; yet to come up out of my own folly I am not strong enough by myself, and I need someone to stretch out a hand

passages.title: On whether the virtues are living beings
passages.text: Fix in yourself as well what I was saying a little earlier: that it is nothing to the point how many people know of your fairness. Anyone who wants his virtue made public is working not for virtue but for glory. Are you unwilling to be just without glory? But, by Hercules, you will often have to be just with a bad name, and then, if you are wise, let a bad reputation well won delight you. Farewell.

passages.title: On whether the virtues are living beings
passages.text: Let him teach me how sacred a thing justice is, which looks to another’s good and asks nothing from itself except to be put to use. Let it have nothing to do with ambition and reputation: let it win its own approval. Let each person convince himself of this before everything: I ought to be just without payment. That is too little. Let him convince himself of this as well: let me be glad to go further and even spend on this most beautiful virtue; let all thought be turned as far as possible away from private advantages. There is no reason for you to look to what the reward of a just act is: there is a greater one in what is just.

passages.title: On gratitude and repaying favours
passages.text: We must do everything to be as grateful as we can. For this good is our own, in the same way that justice is not, as is commonly believed, something that has to do with others: a great part of it comes back to itself. There is no one who, when he does good to another, has not done good to himself. I do not say this because the man who has been helped will want to help and the man who has been defended will want to protect, or because a good example comes back round in a circle to the one who sets it (just as bad examples fall back on their authors, and no pity comes to those who suffer wrongs that they, by doing them, taught could be done), but because the reward of all the virtues is in the virtues themselves. For they are not practised for a prize: the pay for a right deed is to have done it.

passages.title: On choosing guides and applauding philosophers
passages.text: Epicurus says that some people have come out to the truth without anyone’s help, that they themselves have made their own road; these he praises most, the ones whose drive came from themselves, who brought themselves forward. Others, he says, need another’s aid: they will not go if no one has gone ahead, but they will follow well. Metrodorus, he says, is one of these; this too is an outstanding talent, but of the second rank. We are not of that first grade; we are well treated if we are admitted to the second. Do not look down even on the man who can be safe through another’s good offices; this too is a great deal, to want to be saved.

passages.title: On choosing guides and applauding philosophers
passages.text: “It is folly,” you say, “and for folly nothing holds firm, nothing pleases for long.” But how, or when, shall we tear ourselves away from it? No one is strong enough by himself to come up to the surface; someone must stretch out a hand, someone must draw him out.

claims.t: Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good, as an emerald has its own colour. When I act well and am spoken ill of, I do not let the blame or the talk pull me away.
claims.shared: 7.24 and 5.3 both speak of a good act that other people then speak against: in 7.24 it is “to act well and yet be spoken ill of”, in 5.3 a word or deed “that accords with nature” followed by “the blame or the talk” of some people. 7.12 supports “I do not let the blame or the talk pull me away” only in the general sense that I must be good whatever anyone says; the blame and the pull are 5.3’s words.
claims.changed: 5.3 speaks of a word or deed that accords with nature; the claim calls it acting well, in 7.24’s words. 7.12 names gold, emerald and purple; the claim keeps the emerald, the one named in the saying itself.

support.quote: Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good; just as if gold or emerald or purple were always saying this: “Whatever anyone does or says, I must be emerald and have my own colour.”
support.follows: Whatever anyone else does or says, I must still be good, as an emerald must still be an emerald and have its own colour.

I do not let the blame or the talk pull me away

support.follows: To act well and still be spoken ill of befits a king.

am spoken ill of

support.quote: Judge yourself worthy of every word and deed that accords with nature, and do not let the blame or the talk that comes afterwards from some people pull you away
support.follows: When I say or do what accords with nature, the blame and talk that come afterwards from some people should not pull me away from it.

claims.t: Like a headland that stands while the waves break against it, my mind must put itself in order by itself and stand upright, not set upright by anything else, needing no service or quiet from outside.
claims.shared: 3.6 and 7.24 both ask that the mind be right by its own doing and not by another’s: 3.6 “upright, not set upright”, 7.24 “shaped and put in order by itself”. 4.40 gives the image of the headland that stands while the waves break against it; it shares the standing, not the word “upright”.
claims.changed: 7.24 says it is shameful when the mind does not order itself; the claim turns this into what the mind must do. 3.6 speaks of “one” and 4.40 of being like a headland; the claim speaks of my mind. 3.6’s “cheerfulness within” is left out of the claim.

support.quote: while the mind itself is not shaped and put in order by itself
support.follows: The mind ought to shape itself and put itself in order; it is shameful when it does not.

by itself

support.quote: So one must be upright, not set upright.
support.follows: One must stand straight of oneself, not be straightened or propped up by something else.
gives: by itself
stand upright, not set upright by anything else

support.quote: And let there be cheerfulness within, and no need of service from outside, and no need of the quiet that others provide.
support.follows: Cheerfulness should come from within, without needing help from outside or a quiet that others provide.

support.quote: To be like the headland against which the waves break without pause; but it stands, and around it the water that had swelled up is put to sleep.
support.follows: I should be like a headland: the waves break on it without pause, it stands, and the swell around it grows calm.

claims.role: Changing my mind for the truth
claims.t: When someone sets me right and makes it plain that I am judging or acting wrongly, I change my mind gladly, and it is still my own free act. I change only for what is just or of common benefit, not because a view is pleasant or well thought of; what I am looking for is the truth.
claims.shared: 4.10 and 8.14 both speak of changing one’s mind to follow “someone … who sets one right” (8.14: “the one who sets you right”); 6.20 says the same of anyone who can refute me: “I will gladly change”. 4.10 names what may move me, what is just or of common benefit; 6.20 names the truth.
claims.changed: 4.10 speaks of “one” and of two kinds of readiness; the claim keeps the second and says “I”. All three passages use the same Greek verb for changing one’s mind.

support.quote: The second is to change one’s mind, if it turns out that someone is at hand who sets one right and leads one away from some mistaken notion.
support.follows: I should be ready to change my mind when someone is at hand to set me right and lead me away from a mistaken notion.
gives: When someone sets me right
I change my mind

support.quote: But the leading away must always come from something persuasive, as being just or of common benefit, and what is preferred must be of that kind only, not because it appeared pleasant or well thought of.
support.follows: I should change only when persuaded by what is just or of common benefit, never because the new view is pleasant or well regarded.
gives: I change only for what is just or of common benefit, not because a view is pleasant or well thought of

support.quote: Remember that to change your mind, too, and to follow the one who sets you right is no less free.
support.follows: Changing my mind and following the one who sets me right is no less free.
gives: When someone sets me right
I change my mind
it is still my own free act

support.quote: For the activity is yours, carried through according to your own impulse and judgment, and indeed according to your own mind.
support.follows: When I follow someone who corrects me, the act is still mine, done by my own impulse, judgment and mind.

support.quote: If anyone can refute me and make it plain to me that I am not judging or acting rightly, I will gladly change.
support.follows: If anyone shows me plainly that I am judging or acting wrongly, I will change, and gladly.

support.quote: For I am looking for the truth, by which no one was ever harmed; the one who is harmed is the one who persists in their own delusion and ignorance.
support.follows: What I want is the truth, which harms no one; the one harmed is the one who holds on to delusion and ignorance.

claims.t: I fail when I want to be approved of: when I flatter, try to please and show off, or want everyone to praise whatever I do, like a diseased eye that wants only the green things. I could have been rid of these faults long ago.
claims.shared: Both passages name wanting other people’s approval as a fault of the mind: 5.5 “to flatter”, “to try to please, to show off”; 10.35 the mind that says “Let everyone praise whatever I do”.
claims.changed: 5.5 lists approval-seeking among other faults (grumbling, stinginess, blaming the body); the claim keeps only those that seek approval. 10.35 also names the wish that “the little ones be kept safe”, which the claim leaves out.

support.quote: to flatter, to blame your poor body, to try to please, to show off
support.follows: Flattering, trying to please and showing off are among the faults no lack of talent forces on me.
gives: I fail when I want to be approved of
flatter, try to please and show off

support.quote: you could have been rid of these long ago
support.follows: I could have got rid of these faults long ago; nothing in my nature kept me from it.
gives: I could have been rid of these faults long ago

support.quote: “Let everyone praise whatever I do,” is an eye that looks for the green things
support.follows: A mind that says “Let everyone praise whatever I do” is like an eye that looks only for the green things.
gives: I fail when I want to be approved of
want everyone to praise whatever I do, like a diseased eye that wants only the green things

support.quote: The healthy eye must see everything that can be seen, and not say, “I want the green things”; for that belongs to someone whose eyes are diseased.
support.follows: A healthy eye takes in everything there is to see; wanting only the green things is a sign of diseased eyes.
gives: like a diseased eye that wants only the green things

claims.t: I give my whole attention to what another person is saying, and as far as I can I enter into the soul of the one who speaks; and I let every other person enter into my own ruling part, the part of me that judges and decides.
claims.shared: Both passages ask me to go inside the other person: 6.48 “be in the soul of the one who speaks”, 8.58 “enter into each person’s ruling part”. 8.58 also asks the reverse: that I let others enter mine.
claims.changed: 6.48 says “soul”, 8.58 “ruling part”; the claim keeps each passage’s own word.

support.quote: Accustom yourself to be with what another person is saying, without inattention, and, as far as possible, be in the soul of the one who speaks.
support.follows: I should train myself to follow what another person says closely and, as far as I can, be inside the soul of the one speaking.
gives: I give my whole attention to what another person is saying
I enter into
the soul of the one who speaks

support.quote: To enter into each person’s ruling part, and also to allow every other person to enter into one’s own ruling part.
support.follows: I should enter into each person’s ruling part and let every other person enter into mine.
gives: I enter into
let every other person enter into my own ruling part

single.quote: For those people have a ruling part of their own and act on an impulse of their own. You, for your part, do not look round at those things
single.label: Their impulse is their own
single.t: The people who blame me have a ruling part of their own and act on an impulse of their own, and I do not look round at those things.
single.why: It is the one reason the section gives for not heeding blame, and only 5.3 gives it.
single.follows: Other people judge and act from their own minds and impulses, and I need not keep looking at what moves them.

single.quote: go the straight road right through, following your own nature and the common nature; and the road of these two is one.
single.label: One road
single.t: I go straight on, following my own nature and the common nature, and these two have one road.
single.why: Only this passage joins my own nature to the common nature.
single.follows: I should go straight on following my own nature and the common nature, and the two take one road.

single.quote: No longer to discuss at all what the good man is like, but to be one.
single.label: Being, not discussing
single.t: I no longer discuss at all what kind of man the good man is; I set myself to be one.
single.why: Only this passage sets being good against talking about it. It is kept as a rule for what I do.
single.follows: The time for discussing what a good man is has ended; what is left is to be one.

single.quote: Offer those, then, which are wholly in your power: being genuine, dignity, bearing hard work, not loving pleasure, not complaining of your lot, needing little, kindness, freedom, plainness, no idle talk, greatness. Do you not see how many things you are already able to offer, for which lack of natural gift or unfitness is no excuse, and yet you still stay down below of your own will?
single.label: What is in my power
single.t: Much is wholly in my power, and no lack of natural gift excuses me from it: being genuine, dignity, bearing hard work, needing little, kindness, freedom, plainness, and more.
single.why: Only this passage lists what is in my power whatever my talents. The sentence shortens its list: not loving pleasure, not complaining of my lot, no idle talk and greatness are in the quote but not here. The faults of seeking approval that 5.5 goes on to name are in claim 4.
single.follows: These qualities depend on no natural gift, so I can show them now and have no excuse for lacking them.

single.quote: If it is not fitting, do not do it; if it is not true, do not say it.
single.label: Fitting and true
single.t: If something is not fitting, I do not do it; if it is not true, I do not say it.
single.why: Only this passage gives the test of fitting and true. The sentence after the test breaks off: “For let your impulse be …”.
single.follows: Before acting I ask whether the act is fitting, and before speaking whether the words are true.

single.quote: To speak, both in the senate and to anyone at all, with decorum, not over-distinctly; to use sound speech.
single.label: A practice · speaking
single.t: Whether in the senate or to anyone at all, I speak with decorum, in a delivery that is not too careful or studied, and what I say is sound.
single.why: Only this passage is about the manner of speaking. The rare Greek word translated “over-distinctly” is uncertain: it may mean a delivery that is too carefully distinct, or a voice that is too piercing.
single.follows: Whether in the senate or with anyone, I should speak with decorum, not with an over-careful delivery, and say what is sound.

single.quote: The body too must be firmly set, and not thrown about, either in movement or in posture. For what the mind provides in the face, keeping it composed and graceful, something of that kind must be required in the whole body as well. But all this must be kept up without affectation.
single.label: A practice · bearing
single.t: As my mind keeps my face composed and graceful, I keep my whole body firm in the same way, in movement and at rest, and without affectation.
single.why: Only this passage turns from the mind to the body. 7.24 also speaks of the mind ordering the face, but uses it to say the mind must order itself.
single.follows: My body should be steady and composed, as my face is when my mind governs it, and none of it should be put on.

members.text:
Whatsoever any man either doth or saith, thou must be good; not for
any man's sake, but for thine own nature's sake; as if either gold, or
the emerald, or purple, should ever be saying to themselves, Whatsoever
any man either doth or saith, I must still be an emerald, and I must
keep my colour.
members.english: Whatever anyone does or says, I must be good; just as if gold or emerald or purple were always saying this: “Whatever anyone does or says, I must be emerald and have my own colour.”
members.greek: Ὅ τι ἄν τις ποιῇ ἢ λέγῃ, ἐμὲ δεῖ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι, ὡς ἂν εἰ ὁ χρυσὸς ἢ ὁ σμάραγδος ἢ ἡ πορφύρα τοῦτο ἀεὶ ἔλεγεν· ὅ τι ἄν τις ποιῇ ἢ λέγῃ, ἐμὲ δεῖ σμάραγδον εἶναι καὶ τὸ ἐμαυτοῦ χρῶμα ἔχειν.

members.text:
Think thyself fit and worthy to speak, or to do anything that is
according to nature, and let not the reproach, or report of some that
may ensue upon it, ever deter thee. If it be right and honest to be
spoken or done, undervalue not thyself so much, as to be discouraged
from it. As for them, they have their own rational over-ruling part, and
their own proper inclination: which thou must not stand and look
about to take notice of, but go on straight, whither both thine own
particular, and the common nature do lead thee; and the way of both
these, is but one.
members.english: Judge yourself worthy of every word and deed that accords with nature, and do not let the blame or the talk that comes afterwards from some people pull you away; but if it is a fine thing to have been done or said, do not judge yourself unworthy of it. For those people have a ruling part of their own and act on an impulse of their own. You, for your part, do not look round at those things, but go the straight road right through, following your own nature and the common nature; and the road of these two is one.
members.greek: Ἄξιον ἑαυτὸν κρῖνε παντὸς λόγου καὶ ἔργου τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν καὶ μή σε περισπάτω ἡ ἐπακολουθοῦσά τινων μέμψις ἢ λόγος, ἀλλά, εἰ καλὸν πεπρᾶχθαι ἢ εἰρῆσθαι, μὴ σεαυτὸν ἀπαξίου. ἐκεῖνοι μὲν γὰρ ἴδιον ἡγεμονικὸν ἔχουσι καὶ ἰδίᾳ ὁρμῇ χρῶνται· ἃ σὺ μὴ περιβλέπου, ἀλλ’ εὐθεῖαν πέραινε ἀκολουθῶν τῇ φύσει τῇ ἰδίᾳ καὶ τῇ κοινῇ, μία δὲ ἀμφοτέρων τούτων ἡ ὁδός.

members.text:
These two rules, thou must have always in a readiness. First, do
nothing at all, but what reason proceeding from that regal and supreme
part, shall for the good and benefit of men, suggest unto thee. And
secondly, if any man that is present shall be able to rectify thee or to
turn thee from some erroneous persuasion, that thou be always ready to
change thy mind, and this change to proceed, not from any respect of any
pleasure or credit thereon depending, but always from some probable
apparent ground of justice, or of some public good thereby to be
furthered; or from some other such inducement.
members.english: One must always have these two kinds of readiness. The first is to do only what the reason of the kingly and lawgiving art suggests, for the benefit of human beings. The second is to change one’s mind, if it turns out that someone is at hand who sets one right and leads one away from some mistaken notion. But the leading away must always come from something persuasive, as being just or of common benefit, and what is preferred must be of that kind only, not because it appeared pleasant or well thought of.
members.greek: Δύο ταύτας ἑτοιμότητας ἔχειν ἀεὶ δεῖ· τὴν μὲν πρὸς τὸ πρᾶξαι μόνον ὅπερ ἂν ὁ τῆς βασιλικῆς καὶ νομοθετικῆς λόγος ὑποβάλλῃ ἐπʼ ὠφελείᾳ ἀνθρώπων· τὴν δὲ πρὸς τὸ μεταθέσθαι, ἐὰν ἄρα τις παρῇ διορθῶν καὶ μετάγων ἀπό τινος οἰήσεως. τὴν μέντοι μεταγωγὴν ἀεὶ ἀπό τινος πιθανότητος, ὡς δικαίου ἢ κοινωφελοῦς, γίνεσθαι καὶ τὰ προηγμένα τοιαῦτα μόνον εἶναι δεῖ, οὐχ ὅτι ἡδὺ ἢ ἔνδοξον ἐφάνη.

members.text:
Whether thou speak in the Senate or whether thou speak to any
particular, let thy speech In always grave and modest. But thou must
not openly and vulgarly observe that sound and exact form of speaking,
concerning that which is truly good and truly civil; the vanity of
the world, and of worldly men: which otherwise truth and reason doth
prescribe.
members.english: To speak, both in the senate and to anyone at all, with decorum, not over-distinctly; to use sound speech.
members.greek: Λαλεῖν καὶ ἐν συγκλήτῳ καὶ πρὸς πάνθ’ ὁντινοῦν κοσμίως, μὴ περιτράνως· ὑγιεῖ λόγῳ χρῆσθαι.

members.text:
No man can admire thee for thy sharp acute language, such is thy
natural disability that way. Be it so: yet there be many other good
things, for the want of which thou canst not plead the want or natural
ability. Let them be seen in thee, which depend wholly from thee;
sincerity, gravity, laboriousness, contempt of pleasures; be not
querulous, be Content with little, be kind, be free; avoid all
superfluity, all vain prattling; be magnanimous. Doest not thou
perceive, how many things there be, which notwithstanding any pretence
of natural indisposition and unfitness, thou mightest have performed and
exhibited, and yet still thou doest voluntarily continue drooping
downwards? Or wilt thou say that it is through defect of thy natural
constitution, that thou art constrained to murmur, to be base and
wretched to flatter; now to accuse, and now to please, and pacify thy
body: to be vainglorious, to be so giddy-headed., and unsettled in thy
thoughts? nay (witnesses be the Gods) of all these thou mightest have
been rid long ago: only, this thou must have been contented with, to
have borne the blame of one that is somewhat slow and dull, wherein thou
must so exercise thyself, as one who neither doth much take to heart
this his natural defect, nor yet pleaseth himself in it.
members.english: They cannot admire your sharpness of mind. So be it. But there are many other things of which you cannot say, “Because I am not made for it by nature.” Offer those, then, which are wholly in your power: being genuine, dignity, bearing hard work, not loving pleasure, not complaining of your lot, needing little, kindness, freedom, plainness, no idle talk, greatness. Do you not see how many things you are already able to offer, for which lack of natural gift or unfitness is no excuse, and yet you still stay down below of your own will? Or are you actually forced to grumble, to be stingy, to flatter, to blame your poor body, to try to please, to show off and to be tossed about so much in your soul, because you were built without natural gift? No, by the gods. Rather, you could have been rid of these long ago, and be faulted only, if at all, for being rather slow and finding things rather hard to follow. And this too you must work on, not disregarding it and not taking pleasure in your dullness.
members.greek: Δριμύτητά σου οὐκ ἔχουσι θαυμάσαι· ἔστω, ἀλλὰ ἕτερα πολλά, ἐφ’ ὧν οὐκ ἔχεις εἰπεῖν· οὐ γὰρ πέφυκα. ἐκεῖνα οὖν παρέχου, ἅπερ ὅλα ἐστὶν ἐπὶ σοί, τὸ ἀκίβδηλον, τὸ σεμνόν, τὸ φερέπονον, τὸ ἀφιλήδονον, τὸ ἀμεμψίμοιρον, τὸ ὀλιγοδεές, τὸ εὐμενές, τὸ ἐλεύθερον, τὸ ἀπέρισσον, τὸ ἀφλύαρον, τὸ μεγαλεῖον. οὐκ αἰσθάνῃ πόσα ἤδη παρέχεσθαι δυνάμενος, ἐφ’ ὧν οὐδεμία ἀφυίας καὶ ἀνεπιτηδειότητος πρόφασις, ὅμως ἔτι κάτω μένεις ἑκών; ἢ καὶ γογγύζειν καὶ γλισχρεύεσθαι καὶ κολακεύειν καὶ τὸ σωμάτιον καταιτιᾶσθαι καὶ ἀρεσκεύεσθαι καὶ περπερεύεσθαι καὶ τοσαῦτα ῥιπτάζεσθαι τῇ ψυχῇ διὰ τὸ ἀφυῶς κατεσκευάσθαι ἀναγκάζῃ; οὐ μὰ τοὺς θεούς, ἀλλὰ τούτων μὲν πάλαι ἀπηλλάχθαι ἐδύνασο, μόνον δέ, εἰ ἄρα, ὡς βραδύτερος καὶ δυσπαρακολουθητότερος καταγινώσκεσθαι. καὶ τοῦτο δὲ ἀσκητέον μὴ παρενθυμουμένῳ μηδὲ ἐμφιληδονοῦντι τῇ νωθείᾳ.

members.text:
Use thyself when any man speaks unto thee, so to hearken unto
him, as that in the interim thou give not way to any other thoughts;
that so thou mayst (as far as is possible) seem fixed and fastened to
his very soul, whosoever he be that speaks unto thee.
members.english: Accustom yourself to be with what another person is saying, without inattention, and, as far as possible, be in the soul of the one who speaks.
members.greek: Ἔθισον σεαυτὸν πρὸς τῷ ὑφ’ ἑτέρου λεγομένῳ γίνεσθαι ἀπαρενθυμήτως καὶ ὡς οἷόν τε ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ τοῦ λέγοντος γίνου.

members.text:
If it be not fitting, do it not. If it be not true, speak it not.
Ever maintain thine own purpose and resolution free from all compulsion
and necessity.
members.english: If it is not fitting, do not do it; if it is not true, do not say it. For let your impulse be …
members.greek: Εἰ μὴ καθήκει, μὴ πράξῃς· εἰ μὴ ἀληθές ἐστι, μὴ εἴπῃς. ἡ γὰρ ὁρμή σου ἔστω

members.text:
Thou must use thyself also to keep thy body fixed and steady;
free from all loose fluctuant either motion, or posture. And as upon thy
face and looks, thy mind hath easily power over them to keep them to
that which is grave and decent; so let it challenge the same power over
the whole body also. But so observe all things in this kind, as that it
be without any manner of affectation.
members.english: The body too must be firmly set, and not thrown about, either in movement or in posture. For what the mind provides in the face, keeping it composed and graceful, something of that kind must be required in the whole body as well. But all this must be kept up without affectation.
members.greek: Δεῖ καὶ τὸ σῶμα πεπηγέναι καὶ μὴ διερρῖφθαι μήτε ἐν κινήσει μήτε ἐν σχέσει. οἷον γάρ τι ἐπὶ τοῦ προσώπου παρέχεται ἡ διάνοια συνεστὼς αὐτὸ καὶ εὔσχημον συντηροῦσα, τοιοῦτο καὶ ἐπὶ ὅλου τοῦ σώματος ἀπαιτητέον. πάντα δὲ ταῦτα σὺν τῷ ἀνεπιτηδεύτῳ φυλακτέα.

members.text:
To be cheerful, and to stand in no need, either of other men's help
or attendance, or of that rest and tranquillity, which thou must be
beholding to others for. Rather like one that is straight of himself, or
hath ever been straight, than one that hath been rectified.
members.english: And let there be cheerfulness within, and no need of service from outside, and no need of the quiet that others provide. So one must be upright, not set upright.
members.greek: ἐνέστω δὲ τὸ φαιδρὸν καὶ τὸ ἀπροσδεὲς τῆς ἔξωθεν ὑπηρεσίας καὶ τὸ ἀπροσδεὲς ἡσυχίας, ἣν ἄλλοι παρέχουσιν. ὀρθὸν οὖν εἶναι χρή, οὐχὶ ὀρθούμενον.

members.text:
Remember, that to change thy mind upon occasion, and to follow him
that is able to rectify thee, is equally ingenuous, as to find out at
the first, what is right and just, without help. For of thee nothing is
required, ti, is beyond the extent of thine own deliberation and jun.
merit, and of thine own understanding.
members.english: Remember that to change your mind, too, and to follow the one who sets you right is no less free. For the activity is yours, carried through according to your own impulse and judgment, and indeed according to your own mind.
members.greek: Μέμνησο ὅτι καὶ τὸ μετατίθεσθαι καὶ ἕπεσθαι τῷ διορθοῦντι ὁμοίως ἐλεύθερόν ἐστι· σὴ γὰρ ἐνέργεια κατὰ τὴν σὴν ὁρμὴν καὶ κρίσιν καὶ δὴ καὶ κατὰ νοῦν τὸν σὸν περαινομένη.

members.text:
Out of Antisthenes. 'It is a princely thing to do well, and to be
ill-spoken of. It is a shameful thing that the face should be subject
unto the mind, to be put into what shape it will, and to be dressed by
it as it will; and that the mind should not bestow so much care upon
herself, as to fashion herself, and to dress herself as best becometh
her.'
members.english:
“It is kingly to act well and yet be spoken ill of.”

It is shameful that the face should be obedient, and be shaped and put in order as the mind commands, while the mind itself is not shaped and put in order by itself.
members.greek:
ʽΒασιλικὸν εὖ μὲν πράττειν, κακῶς δὲ ἀκούειν.ʼ

Αἰσχρόν ἐστι τὸ μὲν πρόσωπον ὑπήκοον εἶναι καὶ σχηματίζεσθαι καὶ κατακοσμεῖσθαι, ὡς κελεύει ἡ διάνοια, αὐτὴν δ’ ὑφ’ ἑαυτῆς μὴ σχηματίζεσθαι καὶ κατακοσμεῖσθαι.

members.why: Obscure: the speaker is not named, and the Greek as given does not settle whether it means judging together with the wisest men or by the wisest standards.
members.text:
If thou beest quick-sighted, be so in matter of judgment, and
best discretion, saith he.
members.english: If you can look keenly, he says, look, judging with the wisest.
members.greek: Εἰ δύνασαι ὀξὺ βλέπειν, βλέπε κρίνων, φησί, σοφωτάτοις.

members.text:
Thou must be like a promontory of the sea, against which though
the waves beat continually, yet it both itself stands, and about it are
those swelling waves stilled and quieted.
members.english: To be like the headland against which the waves break without pause; but it stands, and around it the water that had swelled up is put to sleep.
members.greek: Ὅμοιον εἶναι τῇ ἄκρᾳ, ᾗ διηνεκῶς τὰ κύματα προσρήσσεται· ἡ δὲ ἕστηκε καὶ περὶ αὐτὴν κοιμίζεται τὰ φλεγμήναντα τοῦ ὕδατος.

members.text:
A good eye must be good to see whatsoever is to be seen, and not
green things only. For that is proper to sore eyes. So must a good
ear, and a good smell be ready for whatsoever is either to be heard,
or smelt: and a good stomach as indifferent to all kinds of food, as
a millstone is, to whatsoever she was made for to grind. As ready
therefore must a sound understanding be for whatsoever shall happen. But
he that saith, O that my children might live! and, O that all men might
commend me for whatsoever I do! is an eye that seeks after green things;
or as teeth, after that which is tender.
members.english: The healthy eye must see everything that can be seen, and not say, “I want the green things”; for that belongs to someone whose eyes are diseased. And healthy hearing and healthy smell must be ready for everything that can be heard and smelled, and the healthy stomach must be the same towards all foods, as a mill is towards everything it was built to grind. So too the healthy mind must be ready for everything that happens. But the mind that says, “Let the little ones be kept safe,” and “Let everyone praise whatever I do,” is an eye that looks for the green things, or teeth that look for the soft things.
members.greek: Τὸν ὑγιαίνοντα ὀφθαλμὸν πάντα ὁρᾶν δεῖ τὰ ὁρατὰ καὶ μὴ λέγειν· τὰ χλωρὰ θέλω· τοῦτο γὰρ ὀφθαλμιῶντός ἐστι. καὶ τὴν ὑγιαίνουσαν ἀκοὴν καὶ ὄσφρησιν εἰς πάντα δεῖ τὰ ἀκουστὰ καὶ ὀσφραντὰ ἑτοίμην εἶναι, καὶ τὸν ὑγιαίνοντα στόμαχον πρὸς πάντα τὰ τρόφιμα ὁμοίως ἔχειν ὡς μύλην πρὸς πάντα ὅσα ἀλέσουσα κατεσκεύασται. καὶ τοίνυν τὴν ὑγιαίνουσαν διάνοιαν πρὸς πάντα δεῖ τὰ συμβαίνοντα ἑτοίμην εἶναι, ἡ δὲ λέγουσα· τὰ τεκνία σῳζέσθω, καί· πάντες ὅ τι ἂν πράξω ἐπαινείτωσαν, ὀφθαλμός ἐστι τὰ χλωρὰ ζητῶν ἢ ὀδόντες τὰ ἁπαλά.

members.text:
Make it not any longer a matter of dispute or discourse, what are
the signs and proprieties of a good man, but really and actually to be
such.
members.english: No longer to discuss at all what the good man is like, but to be one.
members.greek: Μηκέθ’ ὅλως περὶ τοῦ οἷόν τινα εἶναι τὸν ἀγαθὸν ἄνδρα διαλέγεσθαι, ἀλλὰ εἶναι τοιοῦτον.

members.text:
To pierce and penetrate into the estate of every one's
understanding that thou hast to do with: as also to make the estate of
thine own open, and penetrable to any other.
members.english: To enter into each person’s ruling part, and also to allow every other person to enter into one’s own ruling part.
members.greek: Εἰσιέναι εἰς τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν ἑκάστου, παρέχειν δὲ καὶ ἑτέρῳ παντὶ εἰσιέναι εἰς τὸ ἑαυτοῦ ἡγεμονικόν.

members.text:
If anybody shall reprove me, and shall make it apparent unto me,
that in any either opinion or action of mine I do err, I will most
gladly retract. For it is the truth that I seek after, by which I am
sure that never any man was hurt; and as sure, that he is hurt that
continueth in any error, or ignorance whatsoever.
members.english: If anyone can refute me and make it plain to me that I am not judging or acting rightly, I will gladly change. For I am looking for the truth, by which no one was ever harmed; the one who is harmed is the one who persists in their own delusion and ignorance.
members.greek: Εἴ τίς με ἐλέγξαι καὶ παραστῆσαί μοι, ὅτι οὐκ ὀρθῶς ὑπολαμβάνω ἢ πράσσω, δύναται, χαίρων μεταθήσομαι· ζητῶ γὰρ τὴν ἀλήθειαν, ὑφ’ ἧς οὐδεὶς πώποτε ἐβλάβη, βλάπτεται δὲ ὁ ἐπιμένων ἐπὶ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ἀπάτης καὶ ἀγνοίας.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 7.12 is 7.15, 4.10 is 4.12, 8.28 is 8.30, 6.48 is 6.53, 12.13 is 12.17, 7.32 is 7.60, 3.6 is 3.5, 8.14 is 8.16, 7.24 is 7.36 and 7.37, 4.40 is 4.49, 8.36 is 8.38, 10.18 is 10.16, 8.58 is 8.61 and 6.20 is 6.21; 5.3, 5.5 and 10.35 are the same.

Changes the title from “Being good for its own sake”. No passage speaks of a motive or of anything’s own sake; they speak of staying good whatever others say, and of changing my mind when someone sets me right.

Reads 5.3’s “word and deed that accords with nature” as acting well, in 7.24’s words, and “the blame or the talk” that follows as being spoken ill of. 7.24’s first sentence is a saying Marcus quotes; it is taken as a rule he adopts.
Reads 3.6’s “upright, not set upright” as standing by oneself, and pairs it with 4.40’s headland that “stands” and with 7.24’s mind that should order itself “by itself”.
articles.limit: The statement joins two halves that the passages do not join: holding firm against talk, and giving way to someone who sets me right. The editor reads them as one rule, that only reasons move me, but no passage says so. The practices of speaking and bearing (8.28, 7.32) and of entering another mind (6.48, 8.58) are loosely tied to the statement. The Why column holds two related demands (my mind must stand by itself; I follow my own and the common nature) and one stated reason, from 5.3: other people have their own ruling part. Article 27’s claim 4 (wanting others’ good opinion goes against myself) is near claim 4 here, and Article 19’s claim 5 (if someone despises me, that is for them to see to) is near claim 1. Article 23 says what claim 1 says, for the case of those I work for speaking ill of me; Article 29 says what claim 2 says, from 7.9 (I am upright on my own, not held upright). Article 12’s claim 2 says I do not spend my life guessing what others say or think unless it serves the common good; claim 5 here, attending to the one who speaks, is that exception at work. What this article adds is being set right: I change my mind for reasons, and only for them.

articles.title: Keeping to one’s craft

statement.t: I keep to my own reason as a doctor keeps to the craft, and attend only to what I am doing now, even when those I work for speak ill of me.

parts.words: I keep to my own reason as a doctor keeps to the craft
attend only to what I am doing now
even when those I work for speak ill of me

statement.kind: A likeness, and a rule of attention with its test
statement.form: 6.32 gives the likeness between a craft and a person’s own reason, in two entries under Why, each said once. The one claim that two passages share is the rule of attention that 9.42 states and 6.50 tests, in the case where the people the work is for speak ill of the one doing it. The statement joins the likeness and the rule with a plain “and”; no passage joins them.
