seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the article gains what Marcus leaves out here: a ground, that what a helmsman answers for is the work and not its success; how far to go along with other people, which 6.32 says only of craftsmen; and, under “When it breaks”, philosophy that hunts for shouts of praise. He backs nothing in the one claim, and he limits the picture it uses: a helmsman’s or a doctor’s skill is for the good of other people, and the wise person’s good is their own as well.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a clause on praise, which he says of philosophy only: my philosophy does not hunt for shouts of praise. His limit falls on the claim that pictures steering and doctoring, not on the statement: the statement’s likeness to a doctor is about holding to a rule, and his limit is about whose good the skill serves.

items.label: why
items.t: What a helmsman has promised me is useful effort, not good luck. A storm hinders the helmsman’s success but not his work.
items.why: 6.50 fixes attention on what keeps those on board safe and says nothing of a voyage that ends badly. Seneca, with the same picture, says what the helmsman answers for: the work, not its success. He says it of the helmsman only; applying it to my own work is left to the reader. Article 2 says of every act that the work is the act itself.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The helmsman did not promise you good luck, but useful effort
support.follows: A helmsman owes those who sail with him useful effort, not good luck.
support.context: In Letter 85, Seneca answers the objection that a storm makes a helmsman worse at his work, as pain might make a wise man worse. “You” is anyone who sails with the helmsman.
gives: What a helmsman has promised me is useful effort, not good luck

support.author: seneca
support.quote: a storm hinders not the helmsman’s work but his success
support.follows: A storm gets in the way of the helmsman’s success; it does not get in the way of his work.
support.context: Letter 85, on whether hardship harms the wise man as a storm harms a helmsman. Seneca’s own answer: a helmsman who can say “never this ship except on a straight course” has done enough for his art.
gives: A storm hinders the helmsman’s success but not his work

items.label: action
items.t: Outwardly I fit in with the customs of the people around me; inside, everything is different. I aim to follow a better life than most people, but not a contrary one, or I would drive away the people I want to see reformed.
items.why: 6.32 says that craftsmen adapt to laymen “up to a point”. It does not apply this to me, and it does not say where the point is or why they adapt at all. Seneca says it of those who practise philosophy: he draws the line between the outward face and what is inside, and gives a reason, that a contrary way of life drives away the people one wants to see reformed.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Inside, let everything be different; let our outward face fit in with the people.
support.follows: A person who practises philosophy should be different from others inside and fit in with them outwardly.
support.context: In Letter 5, Seneca warns Lucilius not to show off his philosophy by odd dress or habits. “Our” refers to those who practise philosophy; “the people” are those they live among, with their customs.
gives: Outwardly I fit in with the customs of the people around me
inside, everything is different

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let us make it our aim to follow a better life than the crowd, not a contrary one: otherwise we drive from us and turn away the people we want to see reformed.
support.follows: The life one follows should be better than the crowd’s but not contrary to it, or it drives away the people one wants to see reformed.
support.context: Letter 5, on living as a philosopher without making a display of it. “The crowd” are ordinary people, whom the philosopher wants to see reformed and must not drive away.
gives: I aim to follow a better life than most people, but not a contrary one
I would drive away the people I want to see reformed

items.label: breaks
items.t: Nothing is more shameful than philosophy that hunts for shouts of praise: a sick man does not praise the doctor who is cutting him. I am not glad to be praised by people whom I could not praise myself.
items.why: 6.50 speaks only of being spoken ill of. Seneca, with the same picture of a healer and the sick, takes the other case, being praised. He says it of philosophy, not of every kind of work, and it shows what failing looks like there: doing philosophy for the sake of the praise.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For what is more shameful than philosophy hunting for shouts? Surely a sick man does not praise the doctor who is cutting him?
support.follows: Philosophy that hunts for shouts is as shameful as anything can be; a sick man does not praise the doctor who is cutting him.
support.context: Letter 52, on choosing teachers: Seneca allows public lecturers only if their purpose is to make people better. The doctor is the philosopher who teaches; the sick man is his hearer.
gives: Nothing is more shameful than philosophy that hunts for shouts
a sick man does not praise the doctor who is cutting him

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Why are you glad to have been praised by these people, whom you cannot yourself praise?
support.follows: There is no reason to be glad of praise from people one cannot praise oneself.
support.context: Letter 52, on philosophers who lecture in public. “You” is a lecturer who leaves the lecture hall cheerful because ignorant people shouted for him.
gives: I am not glad to be praised by people whom I could not praise myself

items.t: Seneca takes the same two crafts as 6.50, the helmsman’s and the doctor’s, and marks where the likeness ends. Their art is for the good of other people, those the one carries and those the other treats. The wise man’s good is shared: it is the good of the people he lives with and his own as well. The limit falls on the picture the claim uses, steering and doctoring, and not on its rule of attention, about which Ep. 85.36 says nothing. It does not contradict Marcus, whose 6.32 implies that a person’s own reason deserves no less respect than the reason of a craft. Seneca is not quite steady on the helmsman: in Ep. 85.33 a storm does not hinder the helmsman’s work, and three sections later it hinders the service he has promised to others.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the helmsman’s art is a good that belongs to others: it is for those he carries, as the doctor’s is for those he treats
support.follows: A helmsman’s art, like a doctor’s, is a good for other people: those the one carries and those the other treats.
support.context: In Letter 85 Seneca argues that hardship harms the wise man less than a storm harms a helmsman. “A good that belongs to others”: the art serves those carried or treated, not the one who practises it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: [The wise man’s] is a shared good: it is both the good of those he lives with and his own.
support.follows: The wise man’s good is the good of the people he lives with and his own as well.
support.context: Letter 85, on the wise man and a helmsman in a storm. The bracketed words are the translation’s: the Latin does not name its subject, the wise man’s good, set against the helmsman’s art.

amend.t: , and my philosophy does not hunt for shouts of praise
; but a helmsman’s or a doctor’s skill serves others, while my good, if I am wise, belongs both to those I live among and to me

passages.title: On rejecting even moderate passions
passages.text: I judge that a different answer should be given: that neither the helmsman’s art nor the actual practice of the art is made worse by any storm. The helmsman did not promise you good luck, but useful effort and the knowledge of how to steer a ship; this knowledge is all the more visible, the more some chance force has stood in his way. Anyone who has been able to say this, “Neptune, never this ship except on a straight course”, has done enough for his art: a storm hinders not the helmsman’s work but his success.

passages.title: On living philosophy without showing off
passages.text: Rough dress, an uncut head of hair, a rather neglected beard, hatred declared on silver, a bed laid on the ground, and whatever else seeks attention by a perverse route: avoid them. The very name of philosophy, even if it is handled with restraint, draws enough ill will: what if we begin to withdraw ourselves from the customs of people? Inside, let everything be different; let our outward face fit in with the people.

passages.title: On living philosophy without showing off
passages.text: Let the toga not gleam, nor be dirty either. Let us not own silver with engraved work of solid gold sunk into it, but let us not think it a sign of frugality to have gone without gold and silver. Let us make it our aim to follow a better life than the crowd, not a contrary one: otherwise we drive from us and turn away the people we want to see reformed. We also make them unwilling to imitate anything of ours, for fear that everything has to be imitated.

passages.title: On choosing guides and applauding philosophers
passages.text: Nor would I, on that account, forbid you to listen also to those whose habit it is to admit the public and lecture, provided that they come out before the crowd with this purpose, to become better and to make others better, and provided they do not practise this to court popularity. For what is more shameful than philosophy hunting for shouts? Surely a sick man does not praise the doctor who is cutting him?

passages.title: On choosing guides and applauding philosophers
passages.text: And how great is the madness of the man whom the shouts of the ignorant send away from the lecture hall cheerful! Why are you glad to have been praised by these people, whom you cannot yourself praise? Fabianus used to lecture to the public, but he was listened to with restraint; from time to time a great shout of praise would break out, but one that the greatness of what he was saying had called forth, not the sound of speech that had glided by softly and without a stumble.

passages.title: On rejecting even moderate passions
passages.text: Next, the helmsman’s art is a good that belongs to others: it is for those he carries, as the doctor’s is for those he treats. [The wise man’s] is a shared good: it is both the good of those he lives with and his own. And so the helmsman, whose service, promised to others, is hindered by a storm, may perhaps be harmed.

claims.t: I attend only to what I am doing now. If I were steering a ship or treating the sick, and the sailors or my patients spoke ill of me, I would still attend to nothing but how to keep those on board safe or make those I was treating healthy.
claims.shared: 9.42 and 6.50 both shut everything else out of attention, and each has its word of exclusion: 9.42 “only” with what is being done now, 6.50 “anything other than” how I myself bring the work about. This is the only part of the claim that both passages say; the steering, the doctoring and the abuse are 6.50’s alone.
claims.changed: 9.42 is an instruction with no subject and 6.50 a question about an imagined case; the claim states both in the first person. 6.50’s “how I myself might bring about” is read as the act being done now. In 9.42 the word “only” covers the act and the instrument together; the claim takes the act, and the instrument stands as a said-once item. 6.32 is not in the claim: it shares the doctor with 6.50 but says nothing of attention.

support.quote: To be occupied only with what is being done now
support.follows: My attention is to stay on what is being done now.
gives: I attend only to what I am doing now

support.quote: If the sailors were speaking ill of me while I was steering, or the sick while I was their doctor, would I be attending to anything other than how I myself might bring about what keeps those on board safe, or what makes those under treatment healthy?
support.follows: If the sailors or the sick spoke ill of me while I steered or treated them, I would still attend only to keeping those on board safe or making the sick well.
gives: I attend only to what I am doing now
If I were steering a ship or treating the sick, and the sailors or my patients spoke ill of me
I would still attend to nothing but how to keep those on board safe or make those I was treating healthy

single.quote: Do you not see how craftsmen in the manual trades adapt themselves to laymen up to a point, but all the same hold on to the reason of their craft and will not agree to abandon it?
single.label: Up to a point
single.t: I look at how craftsmen work: they adapt to people outside the craft up to a point, but they keep to the rule the craft works by and will not give it up.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of adapting to others and of where the adapting stops. It is the first half of 6.32’s argument and says what craftsmen do; the passage does not go on to say that I adapt to others up to a point. 6.50 has people who speak ill, but nobody there asks for anything to be given up, so the two are not joined.
single.follows: Craftsmen fit in with people outside the craft up to a point, but they keep to the craft’s own rule and refuse to give it up.

single.quote: Is it not shocking if the master builder and the doctor are to have more respect for the reason of their own craft than a human being has for their own reason, which a human being shares with the gods?
single.label: My own reason
single.t: It would be shocking if a master builder or a doctor respected the reason of their craft, the rule their work is done by, more than I respect my own reason, which I share with the gods.
single.why: Only this passage gives a ground. It sets the reason of a craft beside a person’s own reason and uses one word, “reason”, for both; the line adds “the rule their work is done by” only to say what the reason of a craft is. It argues from the smaller thing to the greater and does not call reason a craft.
single.follows: A human being’s own reason, shared with the gods, deserves at least the respect a builder or a doctor has for the reason of a craft.

single.quote: and with the instrument through which you act
single.label: The instrument
single.t: In what I am doing now, I also keep my mind on the instrument through which I act.
single.why: Only this passage names an instrument, and it does not say which one: the body, the mind, or the tool in hand. It is kept as a point of attention I can return to at any moment.
single.follows: I am to be occupied also with the instrument through which I act.

members.text:
Dost thou not see, how even those that profess mechanic arts,
though in some respect they be no better than mere idiots, yet they
stick close to the course of their trade, neither can they find in
their heart to decline from it: and is it not a grievous thing that
an architect, or a physician shall respect the course and mysteries of
their profession, more than a man the proper course and condition of his
own nature, reason, which is common to him and to the Gods?
members.english: Do you not see how craftsmen in the manual trades adapt themselves to laymen up to a point, but all the same hold on to the reason of their craft and will not agree to abandon it? Is it not shocking if the master builder and the doctor are to have more respect for the reason of their own craft than a human being has for their own reason, which a human being shares with the gods?
members.greek: Οὐχ ὁρᾷς πῶς οἱ βάναυσοι τεχνῖται ἁρμόζονται μὲν μέχρι τινὸς πρὸς τοὺς ἰδιώτας, οὐδὲν ἧσσον μέντοι ἀντέχονται τοῦ λόγου τῆς τέχνης καὶ τούτου ἀποστῆναι οὐχ ὑπομένουσιν; οὐ δεινὸν εἰ ὁ ἀρχιτέκτων καὶ ὁ ἰατρὸς μᾶλλον αἰδέσονται τὸν τῆς ἰδίας τέχνης λόγον ἢ ὁ ἄνθρωπος τὸν ἑαυτοῦ, ὃς αὐτῷ κοινός ἐστι πρὸς τοὺς θεούς;

members.text:
It is common to all trades and professions to mind and intend that
only, which now they are about, and the instrument whereby they work.
members.english: … is common to every school. To be occupied only with what is being done now, and with the instrument through which you act.
members.greek: πάσης αἱρέσεως κοινόν. πρὸς μόνῳ τῷ νῦν πρασσομένῳ εἶναι καὶ τῷ ὀργάνῳ, δι’ οὗ πράσσεις.

members.text:
Will either passengers, or patients, find fault and complain, either
the one if they be well carried, or the others if well cured? Do they
take care for any more than this; the one, that their shipmaster may
bring them safe to land, and the other, that their physician may effect
their recovery?
members.english: If the sailors were speaking ill of me while I was steering, or the sick while I was their doctor, would I be attending to anything other than how I myself might bring about what keeps those on board safe, or what makes those under treatment healthy?
members.greek: Εἰ κυβερνῶντα οἱ ναῦται ἢ ἰατρεύοντα οἱ κάμνοντες κακῶς ἔλεγον, ἄλλῳ τινὶ ἂν προσεῖχον ἢ πῶς αὐτὸς ἐνεργοίην τὸ τοῖς ἐμπλέουσι σωτήριον ἢ τὸ τοῖς θεραπευομένοις ὑγιεινόν;

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. 6.32 is 6.35 in modern editions and 6.50 is 6.55; 9.42 is the end of 9.41, the last words of one sentence and the sentence after it.

States in the first person what 6.32 only asks. No passage says “I keep to my own reason”: 6.32 sets the reason of a craft beside a person’s own reason and asks whether the second deserves less respect. It does not call reason a craft, and it does not say that I adapt to others as craftsmen do; the “craft” of the title is a picture, not a claim that reason is one.

Reads 6.50 with “I” as the one who attends. The Greek quoted is Leopold’s edition of 1908 in its Perseus copy, which prints the first-person ἐνεργοίην, “I myself might bring about”. Even so, ἂν προσεῖχον can be third person plural, “would they be attending”, with the sailors and the sick still the subject, and the translators’ notes give both that reading and a third-person form of the second verb. Taking ἂν προσεῖχον as first person is allowed by the printed Greek but not required. On the other reading, 6.50 still supports “speak ill of me” but not “I attend only”, and no claim of the article would rest on two passages.

Lets two of the three parts of the statement rest on one passage each: the likeness on 6.32, the abuse on 6.50. This breaks the rule that every part of the statement rests on at least two passages, and is left for the owner to approve: of the section’s three passages only two say the same thing, so no more is available. Does not quote the opening words of 9.42, “… is common to every school”, because their subject comes before the point where the passage begins; places the instrument of 9.42 under Practice, although the Greek leaves open which instrument is meant.
articles.limit: The section’s three passages yield one claim that two of them share, and it depends on reading ἂν προσεῖχον in 6.50 as first person (“would I be attending”), which the printed Greek allows but does not require; on the third-person reading, no claim here rests on two passages. That claim, attending to my work alone when those I work for speak ill of me, is already Article 22’s claim 1 (when I act well and am spoken ill of, I do not let the blame or the talk pull me away), and Article 2 already says that my work is the act itself. What this article adds is only the likeness to a craft from 6.32, that I owe my own reason at least the respect a builder or a doctor gives the reason of the craft, which Article 24’s claim 1 (I treat living as a skill, learned by training) comes near from another side.

articles.title: Training, and the use of reason

statement.t: I treat living as a skill: I learn it by training, I bring reason to it and wait for nothing else, and I use it to face what happens.

parts.words: I treat living as a skill
I learn it by training
I bring reason to it and wait for nothing else
to face what happens

statement.kind: A likeness, with its means and its use
statement.form: Two passages set living beside a trained skill: writing and reading in 11.27, wrestling in 7.33. Claim 1 gives the rule of any skill, that ability comes from training; in the statement, “I learn it by training” rests on 11.27 for living, and on 12.5 only for the general rule. Claim 2 says that using reason does not wait for anything else. Claim 3 says, through the wrestler, what the skill is used for. The statement lists the three side by side, with one link of the editor’s: “I bring reason to it” makes reason something brought to the skill of living, which neither 4.11 nor 4.25 says.

Coming back to my principles and keeping them ready

When someone offends me

Living now as one about to die

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the first two claims gain a second author; the article gains two reasons under “Why”, an exercise of thinking ahead, and three entries under “When it breaks”; and claims 2 and 3 are limited: I need someone to stretch out a hand, and I may fall so long as I get up again.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands, with one restriction: “wait for nothing else” holds for things and not for people, since I need someone to stretch out a hand. It also gains its reason: becoming good is an art, and nature does not give me virtue.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: There is no one who has not gone more bravely to meet what he had long braced himself for and stood up even to hard things if they had been thought over beforehand; the unprepared man, on the other hand, has taken fright at even the lightest things.
piece.follows: People stand up to hard things they have long braced themselves for and thought over beforehand, and the unprepared take fright even at the lightest things.
piece.context: Letter 107, on what life is bound to bring: illness, loss, runaway slaves. To have “long braced himself” is to have thought such things over often and in advance.
gives: I am able only where I have been trained

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: There is no reason for poverty to call us back from philosophy, or even destitution.
piece.follows: Neither poverty nor outright destitution is a reason to leave philosophy.
piece.context: Letter 17, on philosophy and riches: Lucilius wants an income first. Seneca answers that neither poverty nor “destitution”, meaning hunger, is a reason to wait.
gives: without bread

items.label: why
items.role: Born for it, not with it
items.t: Nature does not give me virtue: becoming good is an art. I was born for it but without it, and no mind has it unless it has been trained and taught thoroughly and brought to the highest point by constant exercise.
items.why: Marcus says that ability comes from training and that this holds in life. He does not say in this section why goodness has to be learned at all. Seneca does: nature does not give it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For nature does not give virtue: to become good is an art.
support.follows: Virtue is not given by nature; becoming good is an art.
support.context: Letter 90, on the first human beings. Seneca says they were free of deceit and sturdy but not wise, and this sentence gives his reason.
gives: Nature does not give me virtue: becoming good is an art

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We are born for this, it is true, but without it
support.follows: We are born for virtue, and we are born without it.
support.context: The close of Letter 90, on the first humans, who were innocent out of ignorance. In “born for this”, “this” is virtue, named in the sentence before.
gives: I was born for it but without it

support.author: seneca
support.quote: virtue does not come to a mind unless that mind has been trained and taught thoroughly and brought to the highest point by constant exercise.
support.follows: A mind has virtue only after it has been trained, taught thoroughly and brought to the highest point by constant exercise.
support.context: The conclusion of Letter 90: the first humans did no wrong because they knew no wrong, and that is not virtue. Seneca then says what virtue requires.
gives: no mind has it unless it has been trained and taught thoroughly and brought to the highest point by constant exercise

items.label: why
items.t: The art of living is unlike the other arts. They deal with the equipment of life and not with the whole of life; and in this one going wrong willingly is more shameful than going wrong by accident.
items.why: Marcus says that the rule of writing and reading holds “much more” in life, and stops there. Seneca also speaks of an art of living, and he says where its likeness to the other arts ends. He leaves untouched the rule that ability comes from training, so this adds to the first claim and does not limit it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Do you want to know how different the condition of the other arts is from that of this one?
support.follows: The condition of the art of life is unlike that of the other arts.
support.context: Letter 95, on whether precepts are enough to teach wisdom. By “this one” Seneca means the art of life, which he sets apart from the pilot’s and other crafts.
gives: The art of living is unlike the other arts

support.author: seneca
support.quote: All those arts are occupied with the equipment of life, not with the whole of life
support.follows: The other arts concern things used in living, and not the whole of life.
support.context: Letter 95: an objector says the pilot’s craft is learned from precepts, so the art of living can be too. By “those arts” Seneca means the pilot’s and the other crafts.
gives: They deal with the equipment of life and not with the whole of life

support.author: seneca
support.quote: But in this art of living the fault of those who go wrong willingly is the more shameful.
support.follows: In the art of living, going wrong willingly is worse than going wrong by accident.
support.context: Seneca’s example in Letter 95: a grammarian is less ashamed of a grammar mistake made knowingly than of one made unknowingly. In the art of living it is reversed.
gives: in this one going wrong willingly is more shameful than going wrong by accident

items.label: practice
items.t: I keep thinking about what may come, so that nothing is unexpected for me and I meet no trouble as a new recruit.
items.why: Marcus’s one exercise here is to practise what I have given up on (12.5), and his art of living stands ready for things that are “not foreseen” (7.33). Seneca’s exercise starts earlier: by thinking ahead he tries to leave nothing unexpected. Article 3 already has this exercise from Letters 91, 76 and 78; here it stands beside Marcus’s “not foreseen”.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We must see to it that nothing is unexpected for us
support.follows: We should arrange that nothing takes us by surprise.
support.context: Letter 107: Lucilius is upset that his slaves have run away. Seneca tells him to expect such things; what must not be “unexpected” is any of life’s troubles.
gives: nothing is unexpected for me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: constant thought will secure this: that you meet no trouble as a new recruit
support.follows: Constant thought ensures that a person meets no trouble as a raw beginner.
support.context: Letter 107, on preparing the mind for what life brings. The “constant thought” is thinking about troubles before they come; the “new recruit” is the unprepared.
gives: I keep thinking about what may come
I meet no trouble as a new recruit

items.label: breaks
items.t: I lay hands on today, and then I depend less on tomorrow. Philosophy, which I have been putting off until I have enough money, should come first: I begin with it.
items.why: 8.21 names the fault, preferring tomorrow to today, and gives no way back. Seneca gives one: lay hands on today, and begin with the thing I was putting off. The excuse “until I have enough” is from the sentence before the quoted words of Letter 17, where Lucilius says he does not yet have enough.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: you will depend less on tomorrow, if you lay hands on today
support.follows: Whoever lays hands on today depends less on tomorrow.
support.context: The first letter, on saving one’s time: most of life slips away unused. To “lay hands on today” is to take hold of this day’s hours.
gives: I lay hands on today, and then I depend less on tomorrow

support.author: seneca
support.quote: nothing should be acquired before this thing that you put off and acquire after everything else; one must begin with this
support.follows: What is being put off until after everything else should be acquired first: one must begin with it.
support.context: Letter 17: Lucilius will turn to philosophy once he has gained enough money. By “this thing” Seneca means that devotion to philosophy, which he tells him to put first.
gives: which I have been putting off
should come first
I begin with it

items.label: breaks
items.t: It is no use to me to control a horse with the bridle if my own passions drag me away, or to beat many at wrestling or boxing and yet be beaten by a hot temper.
items.why: 7.28 says what being better at throwing an opponent leaves unimproved. Seneca says the same of the wrestler and the rider, and names what defeats them: their own temper and passions.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: for what use is it to control a horse and moderate its pace with the bridle, yet be dragged away by the most unbridled passions? What use is it to beat many at wrestling or boxing, yet be beaten by a hot temper?
support.follows: Mastering a horse or beating opponents is no use to someone whose passions drag him away and whom his own temper beats.
support.context: Letter 88, on which studies make a person good. Seneca has just said that neither athletic training nor the old Roman drill with horse and weapons teaches virtue.
gives: It is no use to me to control a horse with the bridle if my own passions drag me away
to beat many at wrestling or boxing and yet be beaten by a hot temper

items.label: breaks
items.role: While I am not yet able
items.t: While my training has not yet made me able, I do not demand of myself, who am still making progress, what is demanded of a wise man. I press on and persevere: a great part of progress is wanting to make progress.
items.why: Marcus shows one failure here, putting it off (8.21), and does not say how to go on while the training has not yet taken. Seneca admits that his own has not, and says how: whoever is still making progress is not to be held to what is asked of a wise man, and presses on. He takes for granted that training is the way, so this stands under “When it breaks” and not under “If I doubt it”. The opening clause comes from the end of Ep. 71.30, outside the quoted words, where Seneca says he would not yet have the things he praises so ready or so practised that they would run out to meet whatever happens.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the fault is ours, who demand the same thing of the wise man and of the man who is making progress
support.follows: A man who is making progress should not be held to what is asked of a wise man.
support.context: Letter 71: Seneca grants that many who professed wisdom have been terrified by the slightest threats, and admits that he still urges on himself what he praises and has “not yet convinced” himself.
gives: I do not demand of myself, who am still making progress, what is demanded of a wise man

support.author: seneca
support.quote: So let us press on and persevere. More remains than we have got through, but a great part of progress is wanting to make progress.
support.follows: One should press on and persevere: more remains than has been got through, but wanting to make progress is a great part of progress.
support.context: Near the end of Letter 71: whoever is short of perfection slips back unless he keeps struggling ahead. What “remains” is the way to wisdom, more of it ahead than behind.
gives: I press on and persevere
a great part of progress is wanting to make progress

items.t: Seneca agrees that nothing outside me is needed: whatever can make me good is with me (Ep. 80.3). But he also says that no one is strong enough by himself to come up to the surface out of folly; someone must stretch out a hand, and Seneca counts himself among those who need one (Ep. 52.2–3). Read in context, the two do not conflict: 80.3 says the mind needs none of the equipment and expense an athlete needs, and 52.2 is about needing a teacher. This limits “does not wait for anything else” to things and does not extend it to people, and Marcus’s own 11.27 says that I am given the rules before I give them.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: No one is strong enough by himself to come up to the surface; someone must stretch out a hand, someone must draw him out.
support.follows: Nobody is strong enough to get clear of folly alone; each needs someone to help him out.
support.context: Letter 52, on choosing a teacher. To “come up to the surface” is to get clear of folly: the wavering between plans and wishes that Seneca has just described in himself and in Lucilius.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We are not of that first grade; we are well treated if we are admitted to the second.
support.follows: Seneca puts himself among those who need another’s help, not among those who find the way alone.
support.context: Letter 52, on choosing a teacher. In Epicurus’s grades the first reach the truth without anyone’s help and the second need another’s aid. “We” are Seneca and Lucilius.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Whatever can make you good is with you.
support.follows: Whatever can make a person good, he has with him.
support.context: Letter 80: Seneca contrasts athletes, who need food, drink, oil and long labour, with the mind, which feeds and trains itself. “You” is Lucilius, or anyone.

items.t: Marcus’s art of living “does not fall”. Seneca’s fighter does: the one who goes down to the fight with great hope has been thrown down without throwing away his spirit, and has got up every time he has fallen (Ep. 13.2). In Ep. 80.3 even the mind may be thrown down and trampled on; what Seneca asks is that it be unconquered and that it rise up. This limits “not to fall”: for Seneca falling is allowed, and what is not allowed is to stay down.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: who, thrown down, has not thrown away his spirit, who has got up more defiant every time he has fallen
support.follows: The contestant who goes into the fight with great hope is one who has been thrown down without losing heart and gets up every time he falls.
support.context: Letter 13: Seneca tells Lucilius that one’s powers are proved only by hard tests. The athlete is his figure for a person contending with Fortune.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: so that thrown down, so that trampled on, it rises up
support.follows: The mind can be strengthened so that it rises up after being thrown down and trampled on.
support.context: Letter 80: Seneca hears cheering from the stadium and asks: if a fighter’s body can be trained to take blows, how much more easily can the mind be strengthened? “It” is the mind.

; but I do not come up out of my folly by my own strength alone: I need someone to stretch out a hand
; yet every time I fall I get up again

passages.title: On accepting fate willingly
passages.text: There is no one who has not gone more bravely to meet what he had long braced himself for and stood up even to hard things if they had been thought over beforehand; the unprepared man, on the other hand, has taken fright at even the lightest things. We must see to it that nothing is unexpected for us; and because all things are heavier for being new, constant thought will secure this: that you meet no trouble as a new recruit.

passages.title: On not postponing philosophy for money
passages.text: There is no reason for poverty to call us back from philosophy, or even destitution. For those who hurry towards this must bear even hunger. Some have borne it in sieges, and what other reward was there for that endurance than not falling into the conqueror’s power? How much greater is this that is promised: unending freedom, and fear of no one, neither man nor god. Should one not come to these things even hungry?

passages.title: On philosophy and the invention of crafts
passages.text: But although their life was outstanding and free of deceit, they were not wise men, since that name now belongs to the greatest of works. Still, I would not deny that they were men of lofty spirit and, so to speak, fresh from the gods; for there is no doubt that the world brought forth better things when it was not yet worn out with bearing. But while all of them had an inborn character that was stronger and readier for toil, their natural abilities were not, in all of them, brought to completion. For nature does not give virtue: to become good is an art.

passages.title: On philosophy and the invention of crafts
passages.text: What then? They were innocent through ignorance of things; but it makes a great difference whether someone does not want to do wrong or does not know how. They lacked justice, they lacked prudence, they lacked self-control and courage. Their unschooled life had certain things that resembled all these virtues: virtue does not come to a mind unless that mind has been trained and taught thoroughly and brought to the highest point by constant exercise. We are born for this, it is true, but without it, and even in the best people, before you school them, there is the material of virtue, not virtue. Farewell.

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: All those arts are occupied with the equipment of life, not with the whole of life; and so many things check them from outside and hinder them: hope, desire, fear. But this one, which professes the art of life, cannot be prevented by anything from exercising itself, for it shatters hindrances and tosses aside what stands in its way. Do you want to know how different the condition of the other arts is from that of this one? In them it is more excusable to go wrong on purpose than by accident; in this one the greatest fault is to do wrong of one’s own accord.

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: What I mean is this. A grammarian will not blush at a mistake in grammar if he made it knowingly; he will blush if he made it unknowingly. If a doctor does not realise that his patient is failing, he goes wrong more, as far as his art is concerned, than if he pretends not to realise it. But in this art of living the fault of those who go wrong willingly is the more shameful. Add now that most arts too, or rather the most liberal arts of them all, have their own doctrines, not only precepts, as medicine does; and so there is one school of Hippocrates, another of Asclepiades, another of Themison.

passages.title: On valuing and saving your time
passages.text: Who will you give me who sets any price on time, who puts a value on a day, who understands that he is dying every day? For we are mistaken in looking ahead to death: a great part of it has already gone by; whatever of our lifetime lies behind us, death holds. So do, my Lucilius, what you write you are doing: take hold of every hour. In this way you will depend less on tomorrow, if you lay hands on today.

passages.title: On not postponing philosophy for money
passages.text: If you want to have time for your mind, you must either be poor or be like a poor man. Wholesome study cannot be carried on without a concern for frugality; and frugality is voluntary poverty. So away with those excuses: “I do not yet have as much as is enough; if I reach that sum, then I will give myself wholly to philosophy.” And yet nothing should be acquired before this thing that you put off and acquire after everything else; one must begin with this. “I want,” you say, “to acquire something to live on.” At the same time learn to acquire as well: if something forbids you to live well, it does not forbid you to die well.

passages.title: On the limits of liberal studies
passages.text: For what is there that is liberal, I ask you, about those people who vomit on an empty stomach, whose bodies are stuffed fat and whose minds are thin and sluggish? Or do we believe that this is a liberal study for our youth, whom our ancestors trained upright, to throw javelins, to hurl a stake, to ride a horse, to handle weapons? They taught their children nothing that had to be learned lying down. But neither these arts nor those teach or nourish virtue; for what use is it to control a horse and moderate its pace with the bridle, yet be dragged away by the most unbridled passions? What use is it to beat many at wrestling or boxing, yet be beaten by a hot temper?

passages.title: On virtue as the only good
passages.text: The wise man, it is true, conquers fortune by virtue, but many who have professed wisdom have at times been terrified by the slightest threats. Here the fault is ours, who demand the same thing of the wise man and of the man who is making progress. I am still urging the things I praise on myself; I have not yet convinced myself. Even if I had convinced myself, I would not yet have them so ready or so practised that they would run out to meet whatever happens.

passages.title: On virtue as the only good
passages.text: So let us press on and persevere. More remains than we have got through, but a great part of progress is wanting to make progress. This I know of myself: I want to, and I want to with my whole mind. I see that you too have been roused and are hurrying with great force towards the finest things. Let us hurry: only so will life be a gift. Otherwise it is a delay, and a shameful one at that, for those who live among foul things. Let us see to it that all time is ours; but it will not be, unless we have first begun to be our own.

passages.title: On choosing guides and applauding philosophers
passages.text: “It is folly,” you say, “and for folly nothing holds firm, nothing pleases for long.” But how, or when, shall we tear ourselves away from it? No one is strong enough by himself to come up to the surface; someone must stretch out a hand, someone must draw him out.

passages.title: On choosing guides and applauding philosophers
passages.text: Epicurus says that some people have come out to the truth without anyone’s help, that they themselves have made their own road; these he praises most, the ones whose drive came from themselves, who brought themselves forward. Others, he says, need another’s aid: they will not go if no one has gone ahead, but they will follow well. Metrodorus, he says, is one of these; this too is an outstanding talent, but of the second rank. We are not of that first grade; we are well treated if we are admitted to the second. Do not look down even on the man who can be safe through another’s good offices; this too is a great deal, to want to be saved.

passages.title: On training the mind and false happiness
passages.text: What I turn over most in my own thoughts is this: if the body can be brought by training to this endurance, by which it bears the fists and equally the kicks of more than one man, by which someone lasts out the day, bearing up under the most blazing sun in the most scorching dust and drenched in his own blood, how much more easily the mind can be strengthened so that it takes the blows of Fortune unconquered, so that thrown down, so that trampled on, it rises up. For the body needs many things in order to be in good condition: the mind grows from itself, feeds itself, trains itself. Those men need much food, much drink, much oil, and long labour besides: virtue will come to you without equipment, without expense. Whatever can make you good is with you.

passages.title: On needless fears about the future
passages.text: An athlete who has never been beaten black and blue cannot bring great courage to the contest. The one who has seen his own blood, whose teeth have rattled under a fist, the one who has been tripped and has taken his opponent on the whole of his body, who, thrown down, has not thrown away his spirit, who has got up more defiant every time he has fallen: he goes down to the fight with great hope.

claims.t: I treat living as a skill, and in a skill I am able only where I have been trained: in writing and reading I do not give the rules before I have been given them, and this holds still more in life.
claims.shared: 12.5 and 11.27 both make ability depend on training that came before it: the left hand holds the bridle firmly “because this is what it has had practice in”, and no one rules in writing and reading before having “been ruled”. The words they both support, “I am able only where I have been trained”, are the editor’s summary of “practice” and “been ruled”. 11.27 and 7.33 both set living beside a skill: 11.27 carries the rule of writing and reading over to life, and 7.33 speaks of “the art of living”.
claims.changed: 12.5 speaks of a hand and 11.27 of writing and reading; the claim puts both under “a skill”. 11.27’s “rule” and “been ruled” are written out as giving the rules and being given them: the master and the pupil of the translators’ note. 12.5 does not speak of living; only 11.27 says “in life”.

support.quote: the left hand, though for lack of practice it is no good at anything else, holds the bridle more firmly than the right, because this is what it has had practice in
support.follows: A hand that is no good at anything else is the stronger one at the single thing it has practised.
gives: in a skill I am able only where I have been trained

support.quote: In writing and reading you will not rule before you have been ruled. This is much more so in life.
support.follows: In writing and reading nobody gives the rules before having been given them, and this is even more true of life.
gives: I treat living as a skill
in a skill I am able only where I have been trained

support.follows: Living is called an art, as wrestling and dancing are.

claims.t: Using reason does not wait for anything else. I have it, so I use it, and when it is doing its own work I want nothing more; I hold to it without a tunic, without a book, without bread, and without the nourishment that learning gives.
claims.shared: Both passages turn on what a person has. In 4.11 what he has is reason (“Do you have reason?” “I do.”), and once it is at work there is nothing else to want. In 4.25 the speakers “have no bread” and “do not have” learning’s nourishment, and they hold to reason all the same. Both say “reason”, and in both nothing else has to be there first.
claims.changed: 4.11 is a dialogue and 4.25 a row of philosophers; the claim speaks as “I” throughout. 4.11 says “use” and 4.25 says “hold to”; the claim keeps both verbs. “Does not wait for anything else” is the editor’s summary: 4.11 says there is nothing else to want when reason is doing its work, and 4.25 concedes each lack with “and yet”. Neither says that nothing else is needed. The “so” is 4.11’s “Then”. In 4.25 the first two people “practise philosophy”, one without a tunic and one without a book; only the man without bread and the last speaker “hold to reason”. The claim puts all four under “hold to reason”.

support.quote: “Do you have reason?” “I do.” “Then why do you not use it?
support.follows: Someone who agrees that he has reason is asked why, then, he does not use it.

support.quote: For when it is doing its own work, what else do you want?
support.follows: Once reason is doing its own work, there is nothing else to want.

support.quote: One person practises philosophy without a tunic, another without a book. Here is another, half naked: “I have no bread,” he says, “and yet I hold to reason.” And I, for my part, do not have the nourishment that comes from learning, and yet I hold to reason.
support.follows: People practise philosophy and hold to reason while lacking a tunic, a book, bread, or the nourishment that learning gives.

claims.t: The art of living is more like wrestling than dancing, and what it takes from wrestling is not throwing an opponent. It is to be disciplined in the face of what happens: to stand ready for what falls on me unforeseen, and not to fall.
claims.shared: Both passages take the wrestler as their figure, and both name the same thing to be good at: 7.28 being “disciplined in the face of what happens”, 7.33 standing ready for “the things that fall on it”. The words they both support are “in the face of what happens”.
claims.changed: 7.28 names throwing and 7.33 names standing; neither sets the one against the other. 7.28 does not say that discipline belongs to wrestling: its better thrower is precisely not better disciplined. The claim takes that discipline and 7.33’s standing ready as one thing, which is the editor’s reading. 7.33 speaks of the art of living as “it”; the claim says “me”.

inferences.words: what it takes from wrestling is not
inferences.why: 7.28 only denies that better throwing is better discipline; 7.33 only puts the likeness in standing ready. Setting one against the other is the editor’s step.
7.28 does not call discipline what living takes from wrestling; its better thrower lacks it. Equating it with 7.33’s standing ready is the editor’s step.

single.quote: Practise even the things you have given up on.
single.label: A practice
single.t: I practise even the things I have given up on.
single.why: Only this passage gives the instruction. 11.27 says that training comes first; it does not say to go back to what I have written off.
single.follows: I should practise even what I have given up as hopeless.

single.quote: You deserve these things that are happening to you; you would rather become good tomorrow than be good today.
single.label: Putting it off
single.t: If I would rather become good tomorrow than be good today, I deserve what is happening to me.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of delay. It shows what failing looks like here. The Greek sets the two halves side by side; the “if” that joins them is the editor’s reading.
single.follows: A person who prefers becoming good tomorrow to being good today is told that he deserves what is happening to him.

single.quote: but not more social, nor more modest, nor better disciplined in the face of what happens, nor kinder towards the oversights of those nearby
single.label: Winning without improving
single.t: I can become better at throwing an opponent and be no more social, no more modest, and no kinder towards the oversights of the people near me.
single.why: Only this passage lists what skill at winning leaves unimproved in my dealings with other people. Its one point about what happens is used in the claim on standing ready. The opening words here, “better at throwing an opponent”, come from the start of the same sentence (7.28a).
single.follows: Being better at throwing an opponent is not being more social, more modest, better disciplined, or kinder towards the oversights of those nearby.

of. For the left hand we see, which for the most part lieth idle because

There is, who without so much as a coat; and there is, who without
so much as a book, doth put philosophy in practice. I am half naked,

The art of true living in this world is more like a wrestler's,
than a dancer's practice. For in this they both agree, to teach a man
whatsoever falls upon him, that he may be ready for it, and that nothing
may cast him down.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 12.5 is 12.6, 11.27 is 11.29 and 11.30, 4.11 is 4.13, 4.25 is 4.30, 8.21 is the second half of 8.22, 7.28 is 7.52 and 7.33 is 7.61.

Reads “rule” and “been ruled” in 11.27 as the master and the pupil, and writes it out in the claim as giving the rules and being given them; the same Greek verb can also mean “lead” and “been led”. Leaves out the second half of 11.27, “You are by nature a slave; you have no share in reason.” It is a separate chapter in modern editions (11.30), it reads like a line quoted from a play, Marcus adds no comment, and its last word may mean “speech”.

“I treat living as a skill” is the editor’s wording for what two passages do. 11.27 applies the rule of writing and reading to life; 7.33 says “the art of living”. Neither says in so many words that living is learned as a skill is.

Reads 7.28, which has no subject and no verb, as a general remark: being better at throwing an opponent is not being better in the four ways listed. Setting that throwing against the standing of 7.33, and taking 7.28’s discipline and 7.33’s standing ready as one thing, are marked in the third claim as the editor’s steps.
Keeps “practise even the things I have given up on” (12.5) and the rebuke about tomorrow (8.21) as said once. No second passage says either, though both fit the statement.
articles.limit: Articles 2 and 5 already say that my work is to use reason; this article adds that living is trained like a skill, that using reason does not wait for anything else, and what the skill is used for. Article 6 already has one passage (8.54) about standing and not falling before an obstacle. The first claim is thin: 12.5 speaks of any ability and not of living, only 11.27 says “in life”, and 7.33 adds only the words “the art of living”. The last sentence of 4.25 is read in more than one way: “the nourishment that comes from learning” may be what learning gives the mind, or a living that learning might earn; the article takes the first. Seneca’s exercise of thinking troubles through in advance is already in Article 3, from other letters (Ep. 91.4, 76.34, 78.29); the item from Ep. 107.4 here repeats it. Claims 1 and 2 pull in different directions: 11.27 puts being given the rules before giving them, and 4.25 holds to reason even without the nourishment that learning gives. The article keeps both. Living as a craft is also in Article 11, claim 3 (being good is my craft, with principles kept ready as a doctor keeps his instruments), and in Article 23 (I keep to my own reason as a doctor keeps to the craft); this article adds that the skill is learned by training and that it is used to face what happens. Article 35 already says, with the same Ep. 1.2, that I hurry to become good while it is possible and that I fail by putting things off (claims 3 and 4); here 8.21 is one said-once failure, and Seneca’s way back from delay repeats that ground.

articles.title: What I turn to

statement.t: I keep going back to myself and to philosophy, rest in philosophy and in acting as a member of a community, and toil without complaint.

statement.kind: A habit, what it gives, and the work it serves
statement.form: The claim on going back is the habit, and the claim under Why says what the habit gives. The claim on the one thing wanted names the work and the rest found in it, and the last claim says how that work is done when it is hard, and what Marcus had to stop doing: complaining. The claim on virtue stands beside these and is not in the statement.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, going back into myself and going to philosophy each gain a second author, and the article gains a reason not to complain, justice without payment or glory, the company of the best people of any age and what to do while I am not yet fit to be alone with myself; he limits the going back into myself, and where Marcus waits on the court he would push the things that keep him busy out of the way.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands, with a limit on its first part: for him, going back into myself is for one who is already good, calm and self-controlled. At its end it gains a reason and an addition: complaining would make what I bear heavier, and I ought to be just without payment or glory. His challenge, that I should push the things that keep me busy out of the way, stands under the claim on what going back gives.

piece.quote: Withdraw into yourself as far as you can
piece.follows: Lucilius is told to withdraw into himself as far as he can.

items.label: why
items.t: Complaining adds to what I bear: if I complain I make my own ills heavier for myself; there is nothing evil in the things I complain of except that I am indignant and complain. I am as wretched as I have believed myself to be.
items.why: 8.8 and 9.10 forbid the complaint and give no reason. Seneca gives one: the complaining is itself what weighs. He says it of illness and of losses, not of toil or of life at a court.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Do not make your own ills heavier for yourself and load yourself with complaints
support.follows: Whoever complains makes his own ills heavier, and does it to himself.
support.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness, written out of Seneca’s own sickness. “Your own ills” are the pains of illness; he goes on to say that everything hangs on opinion.

support.quote: there is nothing evil in these things except this one thing, that you are indignant and complain
support.follows: In the things Lucilius complains of there is nothing evil except that he is indignant and complains.

items.label: action
items.t: I ought to be just without payment and without glory, and I want to be glad to go further and even spend on justice. It is nothing to the point how many people know that I am fair, and often I shall have to be just with a bad name.
items.why: 9.10 tells me not to toil as someone who wants to be admired, and stops there. Seneca says the same of justice, the virtue that looks to another person’s good, and goes on to the hard case that Marcus does not name here: doing right and getting a bad name for it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I ought to be just without payment.
support.follows: Each person should be convinced that he ought to be just without any payment for it.
support.context: End of Letter 113. After a dispute on whether the virtues are living things, Seneca turns to justice, which looks to another’s good. Each person is to tell himself these words.

support.follows: A person should wish to be glad to go further and even spend on justice.

items.label: practice
items.t: When I give myself to my friends I do not take myself away from myself, and I do not linger with those with whom a citizen’s duty has thrown me together. I am with the best people of any place or age: I send my mind to them.
items.why: In 6.43 Marcus looks for the likenesses of the virtues in the people he lives with. Seneca turns in thought to the best people of any place or time; he adds a second place to look and does not say that the first is wrong. His refusal to linger with those with whom a citizen’s duty throws him together also sits against 6.10, where Marcus waits on the court.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: When I have given myself to my friends, I still do not take myself away from myself, and I do not linger with those with whom some occasion has thrown me together, or some cause arising from a citizen’s duty
support.follows: Seneca does not take himself away from himself even among friends, and does not linger with people with whom an occasion or a citizen’s duty has thrown him together.
support.context: Letter 62: Seneca denies that business blocks study, since he lends himself to his affairs and does not hand himself over to them. “Myself” here is his own thinking, kept up among others.

support.follows: Seneca keeps company in thought with the best people, wherever and whenever they lived.

items.label: doubt
items.role: If I am not yet fit company
items.t: Until it is safe for me to withdraw to myself, I guard myself by the authority of a person at whose coming even the worst people would suppress their vices. And I look around at people one by one: for each of them it is better to be with anyone at all than with himself.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section asks what to do if going back into myself does not help because of what I find there. Seneca asks it, and answers: until I respect myself, I borrow the authority of a good person and keep company with others.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: guard yourself by the authority of certain men: let it be the famous Cato, or Scipio, or Laelius, or another at whose coming even depraved men would suppress their vices
support.follows: I should guard myself by the authority of a man such as Cato, at whose coming even the worst people would hold back.
support.context: Letter 25 passes on Epicurus’s advice to act as if someone were watching. This guarding is for the time before Lucilius has come to respect himself; after that he may dismiss his minder.
gives: I guard myself by the authority of a person at whose coming even the worst people would suppress their vices

support.author: seneca
support.quote: You need to become unlike the many, until it is safe for you to withdraw to yourself. Look around at people one by one: there is no one for whom it is not better to be with anyone at all than with himself.
support.follows: I need to become unlike the many until it is safe for me to withdraw to myself; and if I look around at people one by one, for each of them it is better to be with anyone at all than with himself.
support.context: End of Letter 25, to Lucilius, who is still making himself someone he can respect. Seneca’s reason follows a few lines on: with himself, such a man is closer to a bad man.

items.t: Seneca passes on Epicurus’s advice to withdraw into myself when I am forced to be in a crowd, and accepts it on one condition: that I am already a good, untroubled and self-controlled person. If I am not, he sends me the other way, from myself into the crowd. This limits the claim on going back into myself and does not contradict it. He is not consistent about it: in Letter 7 he tells Lucilius to withdraw into himself as far as he can, and adds no such condition (Ep. 7.8).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Withdraw into yourself most of all when you are forced to be in a crowd.
support.follows: Epicurus says that being forced into a crowd is the time above all to withdraw into oneself.
support.context: Letter 25. A saying of Epicurus that Seneca promises to begin to allow Lucilius, once Lucilius has made himself someone with some standing in his own eyes.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: if you are a good man, if you are untroubled, if you are self-controlled. Otherwise you must withdraw from yourself into the crowd
support.follows: Withdrawing into myself is right only if I am good, calm and self-controlled; if not, I must withdraw from myself into the crowd.
support.context: End of Letter 25. Seneca repeats Epicurus’s saying about withdrawing into yourself when in a crowd and answers it: he accepts the saying, and the proviso that follows is Seneca’s own.

items.t: Seneca and Marcus both go to philosophy often; they differ over whether to keep the other business at all. Marcus waits on the court as one waits on a stepmother, and philosophy is why the things there seem bearable to him. Seneca tells Lucilius to resist the things that keep him busy and push them out of the way, and calls philosophy the mistress who is present and gives orders. He is not consistent with himself: in Letter 62 he lends himself to affairs without handing himself over to them, which is close to what Marcus does.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We must resist the things that keep us busy: they are not to be untangled but pushed out of the way.
support.follows: The things that keep me busy are to be resisted and pushed aside, not worked through one by one.
support.context: Letter 72, on business as the enemy of philosophy. “The things that keep us busy” are the employments that keep springing up and for which people keep postponing study.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: she is not a thing for leftover hours; she belongs to the regular hours, she is the mistress, she is present and gives orders.
support.follows: Philosophy is for the regular hours, not for leftover hours; she is the mistress, present and giving orders.
support.context: Letter 53: Seneca tells Lucilius to devote himself wholly to philosophy and not to study it in spare time, as a sick man drops his business to get well. “She” is philosophy.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For I do not hand myself over to affairs but lend myself to them
support.follows: Seneca lends himself to his affairs and does not give himself up to them.
support.context: Opening of Letter 62: people pretend that many affairs block their studies. Seneca says of himself that he has time and that wherever he is he is his own.

passages.title: On avoiding the crowd
passages.text: You are bound either to imitate or to hate. But both are to be avoided: do not become like the bad because they are many, and do not become an enemy to many because they are unlike you. Withdraw into yourself as far as you can; keep company with those who will make you better, and let in those whom you in your turn can make better. This works both ways, and people learn while they teach.

passages.title: On the danger people pose to each other
passages.text: What would you gain by living this way? Not that they will not harm you, but that they will not deceive you. But withdraw into philosophy as far as you can: she will shelter you in her bosom, and in her shrine you will be either safe or safer. People do not ram into one another unless they are walking on the same road.

passages.title: On bearing illness and pain
passages.text: Do not make your own ills heavier for yourself and load yourself with complaints: pain is light if opinion has added nothing to it. If, on the other hand, you begin to encourage yourself and to say, “It is nothing, or at least it is slight; let us hold out; it will stop soon”, you will make it light in thinking it so. Everything hangs on opinion; it is not only ambition and extravagance and greed that look to it: we feel pain according to opinion.

passages.title: On accepting hardship without complaint
passages.text: Yet you are indignant at something, or complain, and do not understand that there is nothing evil in these things except this one thing, that you are indignant and complain? If you ask me, I think nothing is wretched for a man except that there is anything in nature which he thinks wretched. I shall not put up with myself on the day when I am not able to put up with something. I am in poor health: it is part of fate. The slaves have taken to their beds, the interest has gone wrong, the house has cracked; losses, wounds, hardships, fears have come rushing in: it commonly happens. That says too little: it had to happen.

passages.title: On bearing illness and pain
passages.text: Everyone is as wretched as he has believed himself to be. I think complaints about past pains should be done away with, and these words too: “No one has ever had it worse. What torments, what great ills I have gone through! No one thought I would get up again. How many times my own people gave me up for lost, how many times the doctors abandoned me! Men put on the rack are not pulled apart like this.” Even if those things are true, they are over: what good does it do to go back over past pains and to be wretched because you have been? And what of the fact that there is no one who does not add a great deal to his own ills and lie to himself? Then again, what was bitter to bear is pleasant to have borne: it is natural to be glad at the end of one’s own ill. So two things must be cut away, both the fear of what is to come and the memory of old trouble: the old trouble no longer concerns me, what is to come does not yet.

passages.title: On whether the virtues are living beings
passages.text: Let him teach me how sacred a thing justice is, which looks to another’s good and asks nothing from itself except to be put to use. Let it have nothing to do with ambition and reputation: let it win its own approval. Let each person convince himself of this before everything: I ought to be just without payment. That is too little. Let him convince himself of this as well: let me be glad to go further and even spend on this most beautiful virtue; let all thought be turned as far as possible away from private advantages. There is no reason for you to look to what the reward of a just act is: there is a greater one in what is just.

passages.title: On whether the virtues are living beings
passages.text: Fix in yourself as well what I was saying a little earlier: that it is nothing to the point how many people know of your fairness. Anyone who wants his virtue made public is working not for virtue but for glory. Are you unwilling to be just without glory? But, by Hercules, you will often have to be just with a bad name, and then, if you are wise, let a bad reputation well won delight you. Farewell.

passages.title: On making time for study anywhere
passages.text: When I have given myself to my friends, I still do not take myself away from myself, and I do not linger with those with whom some occasion has thrown me together, or some cause arising from a citizen’s duty, but I am with all the best men. To them, in whatever place, in whatever age they lived, I send my mind.

passages.title: On reforming friends and imagining a watcher
passages.text: When you have made so much progress that you have respect even for yourself, you may dismiss your minder. Meanwhile guard yourself by the authority of certain men: let it be the famous Cato, or Scipio, or Laelius, or another at whose coming even depraved men would suppress their vices, while you are making yourself the man in whose company you would not dare to do wrong. When you have made yourself that, and have begun to have some standing in your own eyes, I will begin to allow you what the same Epicurus advises: “Withdraw into yourself most of all when you are forced to be in a crowd.”

passages.title: On reforming friends and imagining a watcher
passages.text: You need to become unlike the many, until it is safe for you to withdraw to yourself. Look around at people one by one: there is no one for whom it is not better to be with anyone at all than with himself. “Withdraw into yourself most of all when you are forced to be in a crowd”: if you are a good man, if you are untroubled, if you are self-controlled. Otherwise you must withdraw from yourself into the crowd: there, with yourself, you are closer to a bad man. Farewell.

passages.title: On not letting business postpone philosophy
passages.text: It is not when you have time free that you are to do philosophy, but you are to make time free so that you may do philosophy. Everything else is to be neglected so that we may sit in attendance on philosophy, for which no time is long enough, even if life is drawn out from boyhood to the farthest limits of a human lifetime. It does not matter much whether you give philosophy up or leave it off for a time; for it does not stay where it was interrupted, but, like things stretched tight that spring apart, it runs back all the way to its beginnings, because it has left off being continuous. We must resist the things that keep us busy: they are not to be untangled but pushed out of the way. There is in fact no time that is ill suited to a study that brings health; and yet many do not study in the midst of the things on account of which one ought to study.

passages.title: On hidden faults and giving all to philosophy
passages.text: If you were ill, you would have set aside the care of your property, and your business in the forum would have dropped out of your mind, and you would not think anyone worth so much that you would go down as his advocate during a remission; with your whole mind you would work at this, to be freed from the illness as soon as possible. Well then? Will you not do the same now too? Let go of everything that hinders you and make yourself free for a sound mind: no one reaches it while he is busy. Philosophy exercises her own royal power; she gives out time, she does not accept it; she is not a thing for leftover hours; she belongs to the regular hours, she is the mistress, she is present and gives orders.

passages.title: On making time for study anywhere
passages.text: They are lying, those who want it to look as though the press of business stands between them and liberal studies: they feign occupations, they make more of them, and they are the ones who keep themselves occupied. I have time, Lucilius, I have time, and wherever I am, there I am my own. For I do not hand myself over to affairs but lend myself to them, and I do not go hunting for reasons to waste time. And in whatever place I have come to a stop, there I work on my own thoughts and turn something wholesome over in my mind.

claims.t: I gain by going back. By continually going back I get a firmer hold on the harmony, my inner tuning; I go back often to philosophy and rest in it, and because of philosophy the things at court seem bearable to me, and I seem bearable among them.
claims.shared: Both passages tell me to go back and name what comes of it: 6.9 says “by continually going back” and names “a firmer hold on the harmony”; 6.10 says “Go back here often” and adds that, because of philosophy, “the things there seem bearable to you”.
claims.changed: 6.9 goes back to the harmony and 6.10 to philosophy; the claim keeps them apart. The places I go back to are listed in the claim “Going back, quickly and often”. “My inner tuning” is the editor’s gloss of “the harmony”: in 6.9 the harmony is the tuning of notes, set beside “the rhythm” of the sentence before, and going back to it goes with going back “into yourself”; the passage says neither “my” nor “inner”, and does not say that the harmony is the same as myself. “Because of philosophy” is 6.10’s “Because of it”, the “it” being philosophy; 6.10 does not offer this as the reason for going back. “The things at court” are 6.10’s “the things there”; “there” is the court, named two sentences earlier. “I gain” is the editor’s word.

support.quote: For you will have a firmer hold on the harmony by continually going back to it.
support.follows: Continually going back to the harmony gives a firmer hold on it.
gives: I gain by going back
By continually going back I get a firmer hold on the harmony

support.quote: Go back here often and rest in philosophy. Because of it, the things there seem bearable to you, and you seem bearable among them.
support.follows: Marcus is to go back often to philosophy and rest in it; philosophy is why the court seems bearable to him and he seems bearable there.
gives: I gain by going back
I go back often to philosophy and rest in it, and because of philosophy the things at court seem bearable to me, and I seem bearable among them

claims.t: There is one thing I want and take pleasure in: to act as a member of a community. I move and hold back as civic reason thinks right, and I rest in going from one social act to the next with god in mind.
claims.shared: Both passages say “one thing”, and in both the one thing is acting for a community: “social act” in 6.6, “civic reason” in 9.10. 6.6 makes it the thing to take pleasure in and rest in; 9.10 makes it the thing to want.
claims.changed: 9.10 says “one thing only”; 6.6 has no “only”, and the claim follows 6.6. “To act as a member of a community” is the editor’s summary of “social act” and “civic reason”, which are two different Greek words. For resting in philosophy, 6.10 uses the same Greek verb that 6.6 uses for resting in social acts; no passage says how the two rests are related.

support.quote: Take pleasure in one thing and rest in it: going from one social act to another social act, with god in mind.
support.follows: The one thing to take pleasure in and rest in is going from one act for the common life to the next, with god in mind.

take pleasure in

claims.t: I go back quickly and continually: into myself when circumstances throw me into confusion, stepping out of my rhythm no more than I am forced to; at a run to my own ruling part, the part of me that judges and decides; and to philosophy as to a mother, while I wait on the court as on a stepmother.
claims.shared: 6.9 and 6.10 both say “go back”: “go back quickly into yourself” and “continually going back to your mother”. 6.9 and 9.20 both ask for speed, “quickly” and “Run”, and both send me to what is my own: “yourself” and “your own ruling part”.
claims.changed: 9.20 says “Run to”, not “go back”; the claim lists the ruling part as one more place gone back to, which is the editor’s reading. Only 6.9 says “quickly” and only 6.10 says “continually”; the claim puts both words at its head. “Quickly” for 9.20 rests on the literal “Run”; the same Greek verb in 11.2 (“run to the parts”) may mean no more than turning straight to something. 6.10 does not say in so many words that the court is the stepmother and philosophy the mother; the claim follows the order of its words. 6.9 says “the rhythm”; the claim says “my rhythm”. “The part of me that judges and decides” is the editor’s gloss of “ruling part”, the Stoic name for the governing part of the soul.

support.quote: When circumstances force you to be, as it were, thrown into confusion, go back quickly into yourself, and do not step out of the rhythm more than you are forced to.
support.follows: When circumstances shake me, I should go back into myself quickly and leave the rhythm no more than I am forced to.

quickly

support.quote: If you had a stepmother and a mother at the same time, you would wait on the stepmother, and still you would be continually going back to your mother. That is what the court and philosophy are to you now.
support.follows: Marcus waits on the court as one waits on a stepmother, and keeps going back to philosophy as to a mother.
